10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.035.summary: This study underscores the underestimated role of SVs in human genetics and their potential to advance understanding of human biology and drug discovery.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.035.title: A phenome-wide structural variant map from 467,152 UK Biobank genomes

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.039.abstract: Self-organization generates cellular patterns that guide morphogenesis, but how it regulates collective cell fate remains underexplored. We show that cellular self-organization constrains the propagation of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of oxidative cell death that can otherwise spread as unbounded trigger waves. The spatial patterning of cell density and alignment encodes transcriptional programs, priming cells toward ferroptosis-sensitive or -resistant fates. Low-density, misaligned regions with elevated YAP/TEAD1 activity are sensitive, whereas high-density, aligned regions with increased NRF2 expression form propagation-resistant boundaries. Cell elongation establishes a polarized distribution of oxidizable lipids, creating peroxidation hotspots at the cell poles that promote propagation along cell alignment. In silico and pharmacological perturbations reveal that pattern-dependent susceptibility and polarized lipid organization act together to constrain isotropic waves into spatially confined, anisotropic propagation. These findings identify self-organization as a systems-level mechanism governing collective homeostasis, providing a paradigm to explore how tissue-scale organization regulates cell death in development and disease.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.039.summary: We show that cellular self-organization constrains the propagation of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of oxidative cell death that can otherwise spread as unbounded trigger waves.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.039.title: Cellular self-organization orchestrates ferroptosis propagation

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.040.abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated as a vulnerability in multiple cancers, yet approaches for effectively inducing ferroptosis in vivo are limited. Bypassing conventional strategies targeting the antiferroptotic glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) proteins, we designed metabolic initiators of lipid peroxidation (MILPOs) and developed the compounds WMK-1/2, which contain tetraoxane radical-generating and mitochondria-targeting groups, as de novo ferroptosis inducers. WMK-1 localizes primarily to mitochondria, induces local lipid peroxidation, and impairs oxidative phosphorylation. WMK-1 induces a "mito-ferroptosis" sub-pathway that skips GPX4 inhibition as a prerequisite, can be rescued by lipophilic radical-trapping antioxidants, yet is minimally sensitive to acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) perturbation and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, and evades retinol-mediated protection. Instead, WMK-1-induced cell death requires labile Fe2+ and can be selectively suppressed by ɑ-lipoic acid, an endogenous, mitochondria-resident antioxidant. WMK-1/2 are bioavailable and exhibit significant efficacy in tumor suppression by eliciting ferroptosis in multiple cancer models and augmenting the antitumor effects of immune-checkpoint blockers. Our work provides a protein-targeting-independent metabolic ferroptosis induction strategy for potential cancer therapy.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.040.summary: Our work provides a protein-targeting-independent metabolic ferroptosis induction strategy for potential cancer therapy.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.040.title: Mitochondria-targeted tetraoxanes initiate lipid peroxidation to drive ferroptosis and tumor suppression

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.042.abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) is a major target for pain treatment, but its effectiveness is limited by dangerous side effects. However, the systemic administration of opioids makes it difficult both to decipher their underlying mechanisms of action and to limit drug action to specific receptor subpopulations to isolate therapeutic effects from adverse effects. Here, we develop a reversibly photoswitchable morphinan agonist termed "azo-morphine-3" (AM-3) that interconverts from low to high efficacy in response to light to enable optical control of MOR signaling. Structural analysis of the low ("trans") and high ("cis") efficacy states of AM-3 bound to the MOR reveals distinct binding modes, with each state driving unique ligand, receptor, and G protein dynamics. In mice, AM-3 drives reversible and repeatable optical control of antinociception across pain models with a reduced side effect profile owing to its limited brain accumulation and its ability to be locally activated.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.042.summary: Here, we develop a reversibly photoswitchable morphinan agonist termed "azo-morphine-3" (AM-3) that interconverts from low to high efficacy in response to light to enable optical control of MOR signaling.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.042.title: An opioid efficacy switch for reversible optical control of analgesia

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.043.abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.043.summary: Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.043.title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.044.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.044.summary: Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.044.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.045.abstract: Cellular heterogeneity and plasticity are hallmarks of cancer that contribute to tumor growth and therapy resistance. Here, we investigated metabolic heterogeneity in small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive cancer type with considerable plasticity between neuroendocrine (NE) and non-NE cellular states. Through integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, we identified a universal dependency on exogenous cysteine/cystine (Cys) across all NE/non-NE SCLC cell states. Notably, NE and non-NE cells with low ASCL1 transcription factor levels underwent ferroptosis upon Cys depletion, whereas ASCL1high cells underwent apoptosis while remaining resistant to ferroptosis. This ferroptosis resistance was driven by the direct transcriptional activation of GCH1 by ASCL1, resulting in increased levels of the antioxidants BH4/BH2. Accordingly, combined Cys depletion and inhibition of BH4/BH2 synthesis reduced tumor growth in patient-derived xenografts. These findings demonstrate that metabolic state influences cell-death susceptibility in SCLC and provide a rationale for therapeutic strategies that exploit these metabolic differences.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.045.summary: Here, we investigated metabolic heterogeneity in small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive cancer type with considerable plasticity between neuroendocrine (NE) and non-NE cellular states.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.045.title: Cell-state-specific metabolic networks govern ferroptosis versus apoptosis in small cell lung cancer

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.048.abstract: Sex-based differences in chronic liver disease (CLD) incidence and progression are well documented, yet the mechanistic basis of this sexual disparity remains elusive. Here, leveraging a large-scale metabolomics database comprising 9,254 individuals, we identify the endogenous bile acid, isoursodeoxycholic acid (isoUDCA), as a candidate mediator of female-associated hepatoprotection. We trace the origin of isoUDCA to a bacterial consortium, which is selectively enriched by estrogen through shaping a specialized intestinal microenvironment. Mechanistically, isoUDCA promotes the nuclear accumulation of SREBP2. This upregulates the intracellular transporter STARD4 and its functionally coupled downstream enzyme CYP7B1, thereby facilitating intracellular cholesterol handling and metabolic conversion. Collectively, our findings support a microbiome-bile acid-liver axis that may contribute to sex differences in CLD susceptibility and support further evaluation of isoUDCA as a potential therapeutic intervention.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.048.summary: Collectively, our findings support a microbiome-bile acid-liver axis that may contribute to sex differences in CLD susceptibility and support further evaluation of isoUDCA as a potential therapeutic intervention.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.048.title: A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.050.abstract: A comprehensive cell fate map of mammalian embryogenesis has remained out of reach given the scale, cellular diversity, and non-deterministic nature of development in utero. Here, we use PEtracer to continuously install heritable genetic marks as development progresses, reconstructing lineage trees that resolve ∼75% of cell divisions across >1.4 million cells from 16 replicate embryos. We pair these trees with deep transcriptional profiling to resolve cell fate biases, restriction timing, progenitor pool sizes, and lineage relationships throughout embryogenesis. Using this quantitative reference, we uncover strikingly reproducible lineage architecture between replicate embryos and chart the lineage dynamics driving fate specification across diverse tissues. Specific biological insights include the progressive restriction of neural crest fate, the relative contributions of distinct mesodermal origins to endothelium, and the dynamics of axial elongation. This work provides a foundation for a quantitative and predictive understanding of mammalian development.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.050.summary: Here, we use PEtracer to continuously install heritable genetic marks as development progresses, reconstructing lineage trees that resolve ∼75% of cell divisions across >1.4 million cells from 16 replicate embryos.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.050.title: Comprehensive lineage tracing maps the landscape of cell fate decisions in mouse embryogenesis

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.051.abstract: T cell exhaustion limits the success of cancer immunotherapies, yet the proteomic changes underlying this dysfunctional state remain poorly understood. We integrated transcriptomics, quantitative proteomics, turnover proteomics, and ubiquitin proteomics to construct a multi-omic atlas of T cell exhaustion. These studies identified pathways regulated through transcriptional and post-translational mechanisms, including degradative and nondegradative ubiquitin modifications, and uncovered widespread changes in proteostasis, metabolism, and DNA repair. Major shifts were revealed in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as differential expression of E3 ubiquitin ligases correlates with immunotherapy outcomes. These findings position the collapse of proteostasis as a central, underappreciated feature of T cell exhaustion and reveal opportunities to restore T cell function. We demonstrate that overexpression of the E3 ligase RNF166 enhances T cell persistence in vitro and in vivo. This work defines proteome-turnover dynamics as a critical regulatory layer in progressive T cell dysfunction, with broad implications for advancing cancer immunotherapy through manipulation of E3 ligases.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.051.summary: These findings position the collapse of proteostasis as a central, underappreciated feature of T cell exhaustion and reveal opportunities to restore T cell function.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.051.title: Proteomic atlas of T cell exhaustion defines proteostatic collapse

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.052.abstract: It has been unclear how Roman and later Germanic political control shaped the demography of Iberia and how it differed from other parts of Europe. We report genetic data from 243 ancient individuals dating to 100-800 CE, analyzed alongside 58 previously published individuals. In Roman times, we document an influx of people with ancestry from the Eastern Mediterranean and an influx of North Africans, especially in the center and south. Beginning in the 5th century, Germanic and Alan (Sarmatian) groups assumed political control. Although we identify individuals with Central-Northern European-associated ancestry, including siblings buried ∼725 km apart, the Hispano-Roman population remained continuous in Iberia. These demographic patterns contrast sharply with those in Britain, where major demographic change followed Rome's collapse, and with those in the central Mediterranean, where both periods were associated with profound transformations. Together, these findings highlight regional variation in admixture and continuity across post-Roman Europe.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.052.summary: We report genetic data from 243 ancient individuals dating to 100-800 CE, analyzed alongside 58 previously published individuals.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.052.title: Contrasting demographic impacts of Roman colonization and early medieval migrations in the Iberian Peninsula

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.053.abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated in multiple human diseases, but the lack of bioavailable inducers has limited its physiological study and therapeutic translation. Here, we report KY0418, a selective covalent inhibitor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) featuring an isourea warhead, with high plasma stability and broad tissue distribution after oral dosing in mice. KY0418 specifically targets GPX4SeCys46 to induce ferroptosis hallmarks in human and mouse cancer cell lines, with greater selectivity than existing inhibitors. In a standardizable acute-liver-injury mouse model, KY0418 triggers ferroptotic ultrastructural changes matching those of established inducers, and systemic administration remodels tissue metabolism and generates hydroxyl radicals detectable by a chemiluminescent probe. Subcutaneous tumors from different cancers exhibited variable responses to KY0418 treatment, from no effect to about 70% growth inhibition, but KY0418 consistently eradicated circulating tumor cells and suppressed metastasis across multiple cancer models. These findings position KY0418 as a tool for advancing in vivo ferroptosis research and its clinical translation.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.053.summary: Here, we report KY0418, a selective covalent inhibitor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) featuring an isourea warhead, with high plasma stability and broad tissue distribution after oral dosing in mice.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.053.title: A bioavailable GPX4 inhibitor for ferroptosis induction in vivo and tumor suppression

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.054.abstract: Efficient integration of gene-length cargos in vivo remains challenging. Non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons, which naturally mobilize large DNA segments through an RNA intermediate, could potentially address these limitations. Here, we developed a computational pipeline to systematically identify a diverse set of non-LTR retrotransposons. Extensive engineering generated elements capable of the efficient and stable insertion of reporter genes in human cells using RNA templates introduced in trans, which we term Gene Writers. Gene Writers successfully generated CD19 and CD20 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells ex vivo with robust antitumor activity. Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enabled in vivo CAR-T cell generation and stable B cell depletion in a humanized mouse model. Our study delineates a comprehensive framework for the discovery, engineering, and application of non-LTR retrotransposons and demonstrates their utility for gene-sized cargo delivery in vivo, thereby bridging a critical gap in existing gene therapy modalities.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.054.summary: Here, we developed a computational pipeline to systematically identify a diverse set of non-LTR retrotransposons.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.054.title: In vivo Gene Writing with engineered retrotransposons

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, but immune-related adverse events (irAEs) remain a major, sometimes fatal, limitation, and the lack of robust preclinical models has hindered mechanistic insight. We present the lifestyle-induced susceptibility to irAEs (LISA) model, in which diet-driven metabolic and microbial alterations recreate human-like susceptibility to anti-PD-1 toxicity. LISA recapitulates multi-organ irAEs with immune infiltration and cytokine production, severity depending on sex, age, treatment modality, and immunotherapy response. Mechanistically, dysbiosis marked by Akkermansia muciniphila enrichment accompanies aberrant immune activation, driving regulatory T cell (Treg) fragility and CD8+ cytotoxic effector populations, both observed in patients with irColitis. Dietary reversal, metabolite supplementation, and blocking interferon (IFN)-γ production or signaling in Tregs restored Treg stability and resolved inflammation. Human-to-mouse fecal microbiome transfer interacts with recipient diet to shape susceptibility. Together, these findings identify dietary, microbial, and immune drivers of irAEs, which can be leveraged to improve immunotherapy responses while minimizing toxicity.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055.summary: We present the lifestyle-induced susceptibility to irAEs (LISA) model, in which diet-driven metabolic and microbial alterations recreate human-like susceptibility to anti-PD-1 toxicity.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055.title: Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.057.abstract: Stem cells self-organize into models of early development, but even under carefully controlled conditions, the resulting organoids exhibit substantial "inter-individual" heterogeneity. To explore its origins, we generated monoclonal gastruloids, each derived from a single mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC). Molecular profiling revealed extensive heterogeneity: some gastruloids failed to develop, others were biased toward mesodermal or neural fates, and yet others contained cell types atypical of conventional polyclonal gastruloids. Applying DNA Typewriter, a cell lineage recorder, we identified heritable fate biases arising prior to gastruloid induction and found that more closely related founder mESCs give rise to more phenotypically similar gastruloids. Linking mESC subclones to their descendants' fates revealed cryptic, fate-predictive differences in gene expression and chromatin accessibility, including at imprinted, methylation-sensitive loci linked to developmental potency. Intrinsic, heritable fluctuations in mESC state are therefore an important source of organoid heterogeneity, and DNA Typewriter enables high-resolution lineage trees in stem cell models.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.057.summary: Intrinsic, heritable fluctuations in mESC state are therefore an important source of organoid heterogeneity, and DNA Typewriter enables high-resolution lineage trees in stem cell models.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.057.title: A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.058.abstract: Metabolites are increasingly recognized as circulating molecules that regulate physiology, yet the mechanisms that couple local intracellular production to organism-wide action remain poorly defined. Using the anorexigenic metabolite N-lactoyl-phenylalanine (Lac-Phe) as a model system, we identify the orphan transporter MCT6/SLC16A5 as a physiologic intestinal Lac-Phe exporter. This mechanism controls the extent to which intracellularly synthesized Lac-Phe acquires systemic activity. MCT6 transports Lac-Phe in vitro, mediates Lac-Phe efflux in cells, and is required for maintaining normal circulating Lac-Phe levels in vivo, particularly following metformin treatment or high-intensity exercise. High-fat-diet-fed mice with global or intestinal epithelial-specific deletion of MCT6 exhibit resistance to metformin-associated weight loss. Bypassing the transport defect with exogenous Lac-Phe normalizes the body weight phenotype of MCT6-knockout (KO) mice. These data connect MCT6 to Lac-Phe and gut glycolytic flux and underscore the importance of transporter-mediated release in the conversion of an intracellular metabolic state into a circulating metabolite effector.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.058.summary: These data connect MCT6 to Lac-Phe and gut glycolytic flux and underscore the importance of transporter-mediated release in the conversion of an intracellular metabolic state into a circulating metabolite effector.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.058.title: MCT6 is an intestinal Lac-Phe exporter required for metformin-associated weight loss

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.059.abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 1014 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.059.summary: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.059.title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.060.abstract: DNA's anti-parallel structure presents a topological challenge to the replisome, as leading and lagging strands must be synthesized in opposite directions. How lagging-strand synthesis is coordinated with leading-strand synthesis remains unresolved in eukaryotes. To address this question, we directly visualized the dynamics of lagging-strand polymerases Pol α and Pol δ at active replication forks using single-molecule imaging in Xenopus nuclear extracts. Surprisingly, we find that neither Pol α nor Pol δ is stably tethered to the replisome. Instead, lagging-strand synthesis occurs distributively and entails the rapid recruitment of new molecules of Pol α and Pol δ for each Okazaki fragment. Consequently, leading- and lagging-strand synthesis are not intrinsically coupled. We propose that metazoans solve the problem of anti-parallel replication not by actively coordinating leading- and lagging-strand synthesis, but instead simply by recruiting new polymerases to synthesize each Okazaki fragment.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.060.summary: We propose that metazoans solve the problem of anti-parallel replication not by actively coordinating leading- and lagging-strand synthesis, but instead simply by recruiting new polymerases to synthesize each Okazaki fragment.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.060.title: Metazoan lagging-strand DNA synthesis is distributive

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.061.abstract: Whether a decline in taurine drives aging is debated, and despite high millimolar intracellular concentrations, its function as a potential guardian of cytosolic homeostasis is unclear. Here, we show that aging increases circulating taurine concentrations in humans and mice. Further elevating taurine in aged mice enhances health span, engaging anti-inflammatory pathways previously linked to youthfulness, and reduces mortality from sepsis and inflammasome-mediated inflammation, suggesting an enantiostatic response. Mechanistically, diverse NLRP3-specific "danger signals" induce taurine efflux from macrophages as a proximal step to activate the inflammasome and the resultant pyroptosis. Taurine restoration in macrophages prevents NLRP3-induced trans-Golgi network disassembly, thereby suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Conversely, lowering taurine biosynthesis combined with reduced bioavailability in macrophages exacerbated inflammasome activation. In humans, sustained caloric restriction elevates adipose tissue taurine and is accompanied by lower inflammation. Together, we identify taurine as an immunometabolic rheostat that links danger sensing to NLRP3 inflammasome activation, suggesting taurine-based strategies to alleviate inflammaging and inflammasomopathies.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.061.summary: Here, we show that aging increases circulating taurine concentrations in humans and mice.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.061.title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.062.abstract: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer cells are critical effectors of anti-tumor immunity. Cytotoxic lymphocytes eliminate tumor cells by releasing perforin (Prf1), a pore-forming protein that enables granzymes (Gzms) to enter target cells and trigger both caspase-dependent and -independent cell death. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized, Gzm-independent function of Prf1. We find that Prf1 directly induces tumoral ferroptosis, an iron- and lipid-dependent form of cell death. Mechanistically, Prf1-mediated pore formation drives endocytosis of the transferrin receptor, which increases cellular iron uptake. Prf1 promotes the formation of endosomal-mitochondrial contacts, which leads to mitochondrial iron accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tumor cell ferroptosis. Dietary iron supplementation suppresses tumor progression in murine tumor models in a Prf1-dependent manner. Higher Prf1 expression correlates with improved survival and enhanced response to immune checkpoint blockade in patients with cancer. These findings define a Gzm-independent function of Prf1 as a direct executioner of cancer cell death through ferroptosis.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.062.summary: Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized, Gzm-independent function of Prf1.
10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.062.title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity

10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.063.title: Deep sequencing of 3,367 maize genomes uncovers substantial contribution of rare variants to agronomic traits

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.005.abstract: Mapping how genetic perturbations influence cell fate is key to understanding human development and disease. Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells. The resulting multi-layered regulatory framework captured known associations and enabled functional annotation of regulator-phenotype relationships. Specifically, our atlas revealed that regulators acted within perturbation clusters to govern distinct gene programs that shaped cell fate. As proof of concept, we illustrated several examples. SMYD3 emerged as a negative regulator of long-term regenerative capacity. Analysis of lineage output further identified KMT5B, TRIM24, SETD7, and NSD3 as regulators associated with lineage-biased outputs. Finally, integration with clinical datasets identified PRDM10 as a candidate dependency in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This work establishes a scalable functional genomics platform in a primary human stem cell system.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.005.summary: Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.005.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.006.abstract: Conventional chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T manufacturing requires prolonged ex vivo activation and expansion, which may compromise T cell fitness and promote inflammatory differentiation. Here, we developed PrimeCAR, a 2-day manufacturing strategy combining low-intensity anti-CD3 priming with IL-7 and IL-21. Compared with conventionally manufactured CAR-T cells, PrimeCAR products exhibited a distinct transcriptional state characterized by preserved stemness-associated programs and a PrimeCAR-enriched primed naive T cell (Tn)-like state. Following antigen stimulation, PrimeCAR cells preferentially engaged proliferative programs while limiting exhaustion-associated regulators and inflammatory mediators. Functionally, PrimeCAR cells demonstrated enhanced expansion, persistence, and durable antitumor activity in xenograft models. In investigator-initiated phase I studies of relapsed or refractory B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, PrimeCAR showed encouraging clinical activity with a favorable safety profile. Together, these findings demonstrate that rapid manufacturing with controlled early T cell priming selectively restrains inflammatory programming while preserving CAR-T cell fitness, providing a practical strategy for improving CAR-T manufacturing and therapeutic performance.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.006.summary: Here, we developed PrimeCAR, a 2-day manufacturing strategy combining low-intensity anti-CD3 priming with IL-7 and IL-21.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.006.title: Rapid CAR-T manufacturing with low-intensity priming enhances CAR-T cell fitness and limits inflammatory programming in a phase 1 study

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.010.abstract: Skin fibroblasts exhibit remarkable heterogeneity across their multilayered cutaneous architecture, yet their roles during wound repair remain elusive, mainly due to the lack of layer-specific genetic tools. Here, we employed a dual-recombinase strategy to develop genetic lineage-tracing tools for all five layers of skin fibroblasts: papillary, reticular, hypodermal, panniculus carnosus (PC), and fascia fibroblasts. Our study revealed an intricate spatiotemporal pattern of fibroblast contributions across different wound severities. Temporally, deep wounds elicited a sequential contribution of these fibroblasts in three stages, while superficial wounds involved two. The early-contributing fibroblasts predominantly occupied the wound bed during the closure stage, while subsequently recruited populations mainly entered during tissue remodeling and scar formation. Spatially, as remodeling progressed, fibroblasts reorganized into a hierarchical arrangement closely mirroring their pre-injury spatial distribution. Our study elucidates the coordinated spatiotemporal interplay of fibroblasts during wound repair and may spur novel therapeutic modalities and interventions for cutaneous healing.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.010.summary: Here, we employed a dual-recombinase strategy to develop genetic lineage-tracing tools for all five layers of skin fibroblasts: papillary, reticular, hypodermal, panniculus carnosus (PC), and fascia fibroblasts.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.010.title: Skin fibroblast lineage tracing reveals layer-specific cooperation in wound repair

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.011.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cells-derived pancreatic islet organoids (PIOs) hold promise for treating type 1 diabetes, but poor post-transplant survival due to inadequate vascularization remains a major challenge. Here, we generated vascularized PIOs (VPIOs) by co-culturing PIOs with blood vessel organoids (BVOs), resulting in integrated structures with BVOs-derived capillary networks that penetrate into the islet structures. These blood vessels structurally exhibit fenestrations characteristic of islet-specific endothelium and carry a molecular signature of organotypic vasculature. β cells within the VPIOs display partially enhanced maturation and greater resistance to hypoxia and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Following subcutaneous transplantation into diabetic mice, VPIOs exhibit markedly improved survival, establish vascular connections with the host circulation, and restore long-term normoglycemia. Our work presents a strategy for generating vascularized islet organoids that enhances β cell maturation and tissue-specific blood vessel specification in vitro and, critically, improves graft survival and function in vivo.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.011.summary: Here, we generated vascularized PIOs (VPIOs) by co-culturing PIOs with blood vessel organoids (BVOs), resulting in integrated structures with BVOs-derived capillary networks that penetrate into the islet structures.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.011.title: Organotypic vascularization improves maturation of human stem cell-derived islets and restores normoglycemia in diabetic mice

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.012.abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.012.summary: Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.012.title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen reveals that Wnt signaling regulates lipid accumulation in APOE4 oligodendrocytes

10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.013.abstract: The mechanisms by which hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain long-term (LT) hematopoietic capacity and transition from quiescence remain incompletely understood, limiting their in vitro expansion and applications. Accumulating evidence underscores the importance of maintaining a low protein synthesis rate for HSC function, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified ribosome-associated proteins specifically enriched in HSCs and multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and found that RNA-binding protein gene with multiple splicing (Rbpms) is required for sustaining low protein synthesis rates in HSCs. Rbpms forms biomolecular condensates that sequester translation elongation factors and protein-folding chaperones from ribosomes, slowing translation elongation and ensuring proper protein folding in HSCs. Rbpms deletion led to accelerated protein synthesis, accumulation of misfolded proteins in HSCs, impaired LT hematopoietic reconstitution capacity, accompanied by aberrant exit from quiescence. Our findings unveil a unique mechanism of translation elongation regulation in HSCs and highlight significance of spatial compartmentalization and translational control in HSCs.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.013.summary: Here, we identified ribosome-associated proteins specifically enriched in HSCs and multipotent progenitors (MPPs) and found that RNA-binding protein gene with multiple splicing (Rbpms) is required for sustaining low protein synthesis rates in HSCs.
10.1016/j.stem.2026.09.013.title: Phase separation of Rbpms sequesters translation elongation machinery to preserve hematopoietic stem cell function

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103112.abstract: The KOLF2.1J human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line was created as a reference for neurological disease modeling. Previous genotyping efforts identified several large structural variants (SVs), raising questions about their potential impact on neuronal differentiation. Here, we identified 37 additional SVs using long-read sequencing and optical genome mapping. Additionally, we found that one of the known SVs contained a previously undetected overlap with RYBP, a neurodevelopmental gene. To assess the functional consequences of these SVs, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of day 90 forebrain organoids derived from KOLF2.1J and two independent control iPSC lines. While cell-type composition was preserved, multiple SV-affected genes were differentially expressed and cell-cell adhesion and synapse-related processes were enriched in KOLF2.1J organoids. These findings highlight the importance of robust genetic characterization and multi-line validation for reliable iPSC-based modeling.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103112.summary: Here, we identified 37 additional SVs using long-read sequencing and optical genome mapping.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103112.title: Characterization of structural variants in KOLF2.1J iPSCs and their potential impact on forebrain organoid differentiation

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103114.abstract: Oligodendrocytes play essential roles in central nervous system development and homeostasis, and their dysfunction is a hallmark of numerous neurological disorders. However, human in vitro systems that support oligodendrocyte lineage progression while enabling the study of disease-relevant states remain limited. Here, we establish human spinal cord organoids (hSpO) and cortico-motor assembloids as platforms to model oligodendrocyte development, neuron-glia interactions, and cytokine-induced dysfunction. We show that hSpO generate oligodendrocyte lineage populations that transcriptionally resemble the developing human spinal cord, and oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) that exhibit physiologically relevant behaviors, including migration and monosynaptic neuronal input. Exposure of assembloids to pro-inflammatory cytokines induces transcriptional changes across the oligodendrocyte lineage, characterized by altered lineage progression and acquisition of disease-associated gene expression programs that mirror signatures observed in tissues from patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Together, this work establishes hSpO and assembloids as in vitro systems for studying oligodendrocyte lineage development and disease-associated states in a human multicellular context.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103114.summary: Here, we establish human spinal cord organoids (hSpO) and cortico-motor assembloids as platforms to model oligodendrocyte development, neuron-glia interactions, and cytokine-induced dysfunction.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103114.title: Human spinal cord organoids recapitulate developmental and disease-associated oligodendrocyte lineage signatures

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103115.abstract: Epigenetic regulation of stem cell fate requires tight coordination with cellular metabolism; however, key downstream effectors remain poorly defined. Here, we show that lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) governs metabolic programs essential for stemness in human fetal neural stem cells. LSD1 inhibition induced a pronounced glycolytic shift accompanied by altered lineage commitment, characterized by suppression of neuronal differentiation and promotion of astrocytic fate. Machine learning-based Elastic Net analysis of transcriptomic data identified a subset of metabolic genes, including PLPP2 and CPT1A, which regulate phospholipid metabolism and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, as key downstream effectors of LSD1. Functional perturbation experiments showed that knockdown of these candidates attenuated LSD1 inhibition-induced glycolytic activation and ameliorated distinct differentiation phenotypes. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed LSD1 occupancy at metabolic gene loci, supporting their transcriptional repression by LSD1. Together, these findings identify LSD1 as an epigenetic gatekeeper preserving stemness by restraining glycolysis and inappropriate lineage commitment.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103115.summary: Here, we show that lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) governs metabolic programs essential for stemness in human fetal neural stem cells.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103115.title: Lysine-specific demethylase 1 links metabolism to stemness in human neural stem cells

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103117.abstract: Microbial metabolites affect host physiology, but how they link genetic defects to abnormal stem cell behavior is unclear. In Drosophila, losing Atg4 in progenitors changes the gut microbiota and raises short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as acetate and propionate. These SCFAs increase intracellular acetyl-CoA, which boosts acetylation by inhibiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) and activating multiple histone acetyltransferases. Chromatin immunoprecipitation identifies Socs36E as a direct acetylation target. Socs36E upregulation serves as a feedback brake on EGFR signaling. However, this brake is too weak to stop sustained proliferation, causing intestinal stem cell overgrowth. These phenotypes are abolished in a germ-free niche and can be recapitulated by SCFA-producing bacteria. Our results support a model where niche-derived metabolites drive locus-specific acetylation of Socs36E, modulating a key homeostatic node and influencing stem cell fate decisions.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103117.summary: Our results support a model where niche-derived metabolites drive locus-specific acetylation of Socs36E, modulating a key homeostatic node and influencing stem cell fate decisions.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103117.title: Microbiota-derived SCFAs modulate Socs36E-mediated feedback to regulate intestinal stem cell proliferation upon Atg4 loss in Drosophila

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103118.abstract: Developmental exposures profoundly shape lifelong health by altering disease resilience later in life. One potential cause of increased disease susceptibility is an altered immune system, originating in epigenetically maladaptive hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Here, we establish perinatal nicotine exposure (PNE) as a mouse model of developmental maladaptive immunity, wherein early-life environmental insults permanently alter HSCs. We show that PNE selectively disrupts the establishment of HSCs and tissue-resident, but not circulating, immune cells. Remarkably, the specific decrease of HSCs and lung-resident immune cells persists into adulthood. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed durable molecular reprogramming of adult PNE HSCs, with inverse regulation of positive trained immunity signatures. Functionally, adult PNE offspring challenged with respiratory virus exhibit exacerbated immune maladaptation, marked by increased weight loss, deteriorated lung pathology, hyper-permeability of pulmonary vasculature, tissue-resident macrophage depletion, and exaggerated neutrophil recruitment. Together, our findings establish that PNE imprints durable maladaptive immunity involving changes in HSCs and their progeny, suggesting a hematopoietic origin for the PNE-induced respiratory vulnerability.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103118.summary: Here, we establish perinatal nicotine exposure (PNE) as a mouse model of developmental maladaptive immunity, wherein early-life environmental insults permanently alter HSCs.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103118.title: Perinatal nicotine exposure disrupts hematopoietic stem cell development and elevates influenza severity in adulthood

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103119.abstract: Cell-based regenerative therapies represent a promising platform for muscular dystrophies, but the role of histocompatibility for muscle engraftment remains poorly defined. Given their close genetic relationship to humans, nonhuman primate (NHP) models provide an ideal system to investigate this question. Here, we generated myogenic progenitors from induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines derived from five major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-typed Mauritian-origin cynomolgus macaques (MCMs). Following extensive characterization, one iPSC clone from each donor was selected for transplantation across distinct MHC matching conditions, including fully matched, partially matched, and mismatched recipient-donor pairs. We found that variation in regenerative potential was primarily donor-intrinsic. Strikingly, fully mismatched donor-derived myogenic progenitors exhibiting high regenerative potential consistently outperformed partially and fully matched grafts across recipients. Our results suggest that, under clinically relevant immunosuppression, donor-intrinsic regenerative potential may outweigh histocompatibility as a determinant of early skeletal muscle engraftment, supporting the development of broadly applicable off-the-shelf allogeneic iPSC-based therapies for muscular dystrophies.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103119.summary: Here, we generated myogenic progenitors from induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines derived from five major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-typed Mauritian-origin cynomolgus macaques (MCMs).
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103119.title: Donor-intrinsic regenerative potential outweighs histocompatibility in iPSC-derived skeletal muscle engraftment in nonhuman primates

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103120.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103120.summary: Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103120.title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103121.abstract: Cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) contribute to most cranio-maxillofacial mesenchymal tissues, including the dental ectomesenchyme. However, the developmental relationships between human CNC-derived progenitors and the odontogenic lineage remain incompletely understood. Here, we mapped the single-cell transcriptomic landscape of prenatal human mandibles and reconstructed the putative differentiation trajectories of CNC-derived ectomesenchymal populations. Notably, we identified a distinct population of SLITRK6+ cells enriched in the odontogenic ectomesenchyme. These cells were detected in prenatal tooth germs and postnatal dental progenitor niches, including the apical papilla and dental follicle, but were rare in mature dental tissues. Functionally, SLITRK6+ cells exhibited enhanced clonogenic and odontogenic capacities and supported dentin-like matrix formation, pulp-dentin complex regeneration, and alveolar bone repair. SLITRK6 knockdown impaired odontogenic differentiation and reduced SMAD1/5/9 phosphorylation, suggesting potential involvement of BMP/SMAD signaling. Collectively, these findings identify SLITRK6+ tooth germ ectomesenchymal stem cells as prospectively isolatable progenitor populations associated with human dental development and regeneration.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103121.summary: Here, we mapped the single-cell transcriptomic landscape of prenatal human mandibles and reconstructed the putative differentiation trajectories of CNC-derived ectomesenchymal populations.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103121.title: Identification of human tooth germ ectomesenchymal stem cells

10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103123.abstract: Early human development involves dynamic cell-state transitions, complicating distinction between transient transcriptional changes and stable lineage commitment in human pluripotent stem cell models. To address this challenge, we establish a curated, cross-platform marker framework for pluripotency and early germ-layer identity. Starting from an unbiased RNA-seq discovery set, we validated candidates by qPCR and evaluated the panel across independent bulk RNA-seq and embryonic single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets. This yielded 67 validated markers, of which 66 were retained for downstream transcriptomic analyses. Our framework identified early developmental states across heterogeneous datasets and showed lineage-associated enrichment in human and macaque embryonic references despite substantial transcriptional variability. Protein-level concordance was observed for detectable targets in KOLF2.1J proteomic data. To enable broad application, we introduce DeepDiff, a web-based resource integrating the marker framework and enabling automated fate classification. Together, this work provides a transferable framework for assessing early developmental identity across experimental contexts.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103123.summary: Together, this work provides a transferable framework for assessing early developmental identity across experimental contexts.
10.1016/j.stemcr.2026.103123.title: Defining early human developmental identity: A curated, cross-platform marker framework

10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01296-1.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In hereditary angioedema, a rare bradykinin-mediated condition, oral on-demand treatments facilitating prompt administration and providing rapid, sustained relief and attack resolution remain scant. We investigated the efficacy and safety of deucrictibant, an oral bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist, for on-demand treatment of hereditary angioedema attacks.

METHODS: RAPIDe-3 was a phase 3, double-blind, 2 × 2 crossover trial in adolescent and adult participants (aged ≥12 to <18 years and aged ≥18 to ≤75 years, respectively) with hereditary angioedema, at 59 sites across 24 countries on six continents. Eligible participants had hereditary angioedema, including those with normal C1 inhibitor associated with a documented genetic variant, at least two attacks within the last 3 months before screening, and experience with effectively using conventional on-demand therapies for hereditary angioedema attacks. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to one of two double-blind crossover sequences to treat two attacks with a 20 mg oral deucrictibant immediate-release capsule or placebo as either deucrictibant-placebo or placebo-deucrictibant, stratified by age and use of long-term prophylaxis. The primary endpoint was time to onset of symptom relief, defined as Patient Global Impression of Change rating of at least a little better. Safety was assessed in all participants who received any dose of study drug. RAPIDe-3 is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06343779) and is complete.

FINDINGS: Between April 4, 2024, and Sept 1, 2025, 149 people were assessed for eligibility, and 134 eligible participants (ten [7%] adolescents and 124 [93%] adults) were randomly allocated. 58 (43%) were male and 76 (57%) were female, and the median age was 38·0 years (IQR 27·0-50·0). 113 participants treated 201 attacks. The primary efficacy analysis included 88 participants with paired treated attacks. Of these, 47 (53%) participants were female and 41 (47%) were male, and 60 (68%), 16 (18%), 4 (5%), and 1 (1%) were White, Asian, Black, and American Indian or Alaska Native, respectively. Onset of symptom relief occurred significantly faster with deucrictibant than placebo, with median times of 1·28 h (95% CI 1·05 to 1·52) and more than 12 h (5·82 to >12), respectively (p<0·0001). Fatigue was the only adverse event reported more than once within 3 days post-treatment: a single event was reported by two participants, one of which was deemed unrelated to treatment. Across the study, no treatment-related adverse events were assessed as severe or serious, and no adverse events led to treatment discontinuation.

INTERPRETATION: Oral deucrictibant provided faster times to symptom relief than placebo and was generally well tolerated. These results support the use of deucrictibant as potentially the first orally administered bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist for the treatment of attacks of bradykinin-mediated angioedema, including hereditary angioedema, and may address an unmet need for options that are effective and well tolerated, with convenient administration.

FUNDING: Pharvaris.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01296-1.summary: Oral deucrictibant provided faster times to symptom relief than placebo and was generally well tolerated.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01296-1.title: Oral deucrictibant for on-demand treatment of hereditary angioedema attacks: a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial

10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01480-7.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Persistent haemolytic anaemia and recurrent vaso-occlusion drive complications and accelerate mortality in sickle cell disease. Mitapivat, an oral allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase, increases ATP and decreases 2,3-DPG with the potential to improve haemolytic anaemia and reduce sickling. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of mitapivat in patients with sickle cell disease.

METHODS: We report results from RISE UP, a phase 3, double-blind, global, randomised, placebo-controlled trial from 69 sites across 15 countries. Patients older than 16 years with anaemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises were randomly assigned (2:1) to either mitapivat 100 mg or placebo twice a day using permuted-block randomisation. Primary endpoints, assessed in all randomly assigned patients, were haemoglobin response (≥1·0 g/dL increase in average haemoglobin concentration from week 24 to week 52 compared with baseline) and annualised rate of sickle cell pain crises. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05031780, and the open-label extension is ongoing.

FINDINGS: A total of 207 patients were randomly assigned to mitapivat (138 [67%]) or placebo (69 [33%]). 56 (41%) of 138 patients in the mitapivat group had a haemoglobin response, compared with two (3%) of 69 patients on placebo (adjusted difference 38%, 95% CI 29-47; two-sided p<0·0001). The annualised rate (95% CI) of sickle cell pain crises was 2·6 (2·3-3·0) for mitapivat and 3·1 (2·6-3·6) for placebo (two-sided p=0·1213). Serious adverse events were reported in 28 (20%) patients on mitapivat and 20 (29%) patients on placebo; one (1%) patient and 0 patients, respectively, were deemed treatment related.

INTERPRETATION: Mitapivat, an oral pyruvate kinase activator, with a novel mechanism that ameliorates haemolytic anaemia, has the potential to be an effective and convenient disease-modifying treatment for people with sickle cell disease.

FUNDING: Agios Pharmaceuticals.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01480-7.summary: Mitapivat, an oral pyruvate kinase activator, with a novel mechanism that ameliorates haemolytic anaemia, has the potential to be an effective and convenient disease-modifying treatment for people with sickle cell disease.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01480-7.title: Efficacy and safety of mitapivat in patients with sickle cell disease (RISE UP): a phase 3, double-blind, global, randomised, placebo-controlled trial

10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01535-7.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems show promise for assisting primary care providers (PCPs) with patient care. We aimed to evaluate the safety and quality of clinical conversations of a patient-facing conversational AI system, which engaged in real-world urgent primary care appointments.

METHODS: In this prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study, English-speaking patients aged at least 18 years interacted with the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE) up to 5 days before a single-complaint urgent primary care appointment. Physician safety supervisors monitored all interactions and were trained to intervene on the basis of predefined safety criteria. AMIE transcripts and summaries were shared with PCPs before the visit. Primary outcomes were the number of supervised conversation safety stops, AMIE's conversation quality assessed by clinical evaluators, and patient and PCP experiences per surveys. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06911398).

FINDINGS: From April to November, 2025, 114 patients were enrolled with 98 completing both the AMIE interaction and the PCP appointment. Zero conversation safety stops were required on the basis of prespecified criteria. Safety supervisors noted one hallucination and added clinical information in five interactions. AMIE's conversations were rated favourably in 87-100% of cases (17 criteria) by clinical evaluators, and 48-96% (16 criteria) by patients. Patient attitudes towards AI improved after interacting with AMIE and remained elevated after the patient's visit with their physician. PCPs completed post-surveys in 60 of 98 cases, including 44 cases in which they reviewed the AMIE transcript before the visit. PCPs found AMIE helpful for visit preparation in 33 of 44 cases and reported that it might have changed their behaviour in 25 of 44 cases.

INTERPRETATION: Although further research is needed, this study shows the initial feasibility of conversational AI in a real-world setting-assessed via conversation safety and quality, as well as user acceptance-and represents a crucial step towards clinical translation.

FUNDING: Alphabet.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01535-7.summary: Although further research is needed, this study shows the initial feasibility of conversational AI in a real-world setting-assessed via conversation safety and quality, as well as user acceptance-and represents a crucial step towards clinical translation.
10.1016/s0140-6736(26)01535-7.title: Conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence in ambulatory primary care: a prospective feasibility study

10.1038/s41563-026-02759-4.abstract: Metal-free molecular magnets differ from conventional magnetic devices that predominantly rely on metallic magnets as these metal-free materials may offer biocompatibility and bioresorbability. However, existing molecular materials lack the ferromagnetic strength required for high-fidelity sensing at clinically relevant tissue depths. Here we introduce a bioresorbable metal-free molecular magnet derived from graphitic carbon nitride, combining metallic-level ferromagnetism with full bioresorbability. De-nitrogenation creates spin centres coupled through a reconstructed π-σ conjugated framework, conferring robust spontaneous magnetization that remains stable under physiological conditions. Integrated with poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) and silk fibroin, the material forms catheter-deliverable epicardial patches for cardiac tracking and can also be dispersed in injectable hydrogels for organ-scale sensing, including the three-dimensional reconstruction of localized hepatic pathologies. Coupled with a skin-interfaced Hall array, this magnetic sensing architecture provides the continuous, untethered monitoring of multi-organ dynamics, robust against motion artifacts and tissue impedance. In porcine models, it facilitates the continuous assessment of ejection fraction over 4 weeks, followed by benign bioresorption. Benchmarked against standard-of-care echocardiography, this approach delivers clinical-grade trajectories, supporting longitudinal, infrastructure-independent physiological monitoring.
10.1038/s41563-026-02759-4.summary: Here we introduce a bioresorbable metal-free molecular magnet derived from graphitic carbon nitride, combining metallic-level ferromagnetism with full bioresorbability.
10.1038/s41563-026-02759-4.title: Bioresorbable metal-free molecular magnets enable untethered organ monitoring

10.1038/s41563-026-02775-4.title: Direct imaging elucidates ionic memory in two-dimensional nanochannels

10.1038/s41563-026-02778-1.abstract: Magnonic circuits that use spin waves for nanoscale signal processing and computing are widely regarded as a promising alternative to traditional semiconductor electronics. However, a key missing component of this information nanotechnology is a feasible approach for the integration of memory directly into spin-wave devices. Here we propose a strategy for the implementation of built-in non-volatile memory, which uses the static magnetization states of waveguiding elements within a magnonic network fabricated from a low-loss magnetic insulator and operating at zero bias magnetic field. We show that switching the magnetization direction in these elements enables efficient control over spin-wave propagation paths. Furthermore, we suggest an approach to achieve low-energy selective magnetization switching in such systems. Our results open new possibilities for the realization of advanced, self-contained magnonic nano-circuits.
10.1038/s41563-026-02778-1.summary: Here we propose a strategy for the implementation of built-in non-volatile memory, which uses the static magnetization states of waveguiding elements within a magnonic network fabricated from a low-loss magnetic insulator and operating at zero bias magnetic field.
10.1038/s41563-026-02778-1.title: Zero-field spin-wave networks with integrated non-volatile memory

10.1038/s41563-026-02780-7.title: III-nitride-based in-sensor computing enabled by interfacial polarization effects

10.1038/s41586-026-10733-y.abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2-7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light-electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.
10.1038/s41586-026-10733-y.summary: Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network.
10.1038/s41586-026-10733-y.title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control

10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z.abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199-138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.
10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z.summary: Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.
10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z.title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology

10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8.abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh-wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world's largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.
10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8.summary: We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure.
10.1038/s41586-026-11145-8.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms

10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9.abstract: Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species1-3, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans. Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2-BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington's disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.
10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9.summary: Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.
10.1038/s41586-026-11152-9.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis

10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.
10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4.summary: We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6.
10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes

10.1038/s41586-026-11168-1.abstract: The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation1-5, rising tree mortality6-8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest9-11. Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions1-4,11,12. Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable1,9,13. Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts9,14-17. Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr-1, with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr-1) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011-2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr-1) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019-2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr-1) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr-1) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.
10.1038/s41586-026-11168-1.summary: Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO2 measurements.
10.1038/s41586-026-11168-1.title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts

10.1038/s41586-026-11172-5.abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1-5 and spin-transfer torque6-9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin-split band structure10-13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin-transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm-2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.
10.1038/s41586-026-11172-5.summary: Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT).
10.1038/s41586-026-11172-5.title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions

10.1038/s41586-026-11175-2.abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.
