10.1038/s41586-026-11175-2.summary: Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture…
10.1038/s41586-026-11175-2.title: Functional architecture of the human insula

10.1038/s41586-026-11179-y.abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.
10.1038/s41586-026-11179-y.summary: Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping.
10.1038/s41586-026-11179-y.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root

10.1038/s41586-026-11183-2.abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1-5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6-12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14-18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.
10.1038/s41586-026-11183-2.summary: Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation.
10.1038/s41586-026-11183-2.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement

10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms-occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus-receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.
10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1.summary: Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution.
10.1038/s41586-026-11184-1.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses

10.1038/s41586-026-11186-z.abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51- astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.
10.1038/s41586-026-11186-z.summary: We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus.
10.1038/s41586-026-11186-z.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits

10.1038/s41586-026-11188-x.abstract: WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint1-3. Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53-mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53-wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex-cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/CCDH1). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 (FZR1) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/CCDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.
10.1038/s41586-026-11188-x.summary: Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex-cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/CCDH1).
10.1038/s41586-026-11188-x.title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry

10.1038/s41586-026-11205-z.abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks-a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein-and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.
10.1038/s41586-026-11205-z.summary: Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function.
10.1038/s41586-026-11205-z.title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language

10.1038/s41586-026-11207-x.abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1-6. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C-CH4 = -40.0‰ to -36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.
10.1038/s41586-026-11207-x.summary: Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir.
10.1038/s41586-026-11207-x.title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis

10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x.abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage's polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4-6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.
10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x.summary: Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation.
10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x.title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance

10.1038/s41586-026-11317-6.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.
10.1038/s41586-026-11317-6.summary: These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.
10.1038/s41586-026-11317-6.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts

10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3.abstract: Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA-IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11-0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02-0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.
10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3.summary: Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes.
10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3.title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2

10.1038/s41587-026-03327-6.abstract: Transcriptomic measurement technologies provide powerful approaches to understand biology but are limited to providing either a high-resolution snapshot at a moment in time or a low-resolution history of transcription constrained to a few genes over a narrow time range. Here, we introduce the 'recordanelle', a single-component synthetic organelle capable of recording the transcriptome in human cells. Recordanelles are composed of a mitochondrial membrane anchor, a condensate assembler and a poly(A)-binding protein. We demonstrate that the recordanelle can be engineered to recruit engineered RNAs or a sampling of up to 90% of all endogenous mRNAs and protect them over several days. We further show that transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from inducible promoters or interferon signaling are preserved throughout time within the recordanelle at the single-cell level. This work provides a nondisruptive and unbiased transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording technology to enable a deeper understanding of biology.
10.1038/s41587-026-03327-6.summary: Here, we introduce the 'recordanelle', a single-component synthetic organelle capable of recording the transcriptome in human cells.
10.1038/s41587-026-03327-6.title: Recordanelles for transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording in human cells

10.1038/s41587-026-03348-1.abstract: Here we present DynaVelo, a generative neural ordinary differential equation model that learns the joint dynamics of gene expression and transcription factor (TF) motif activity from single-cell multiome data. DynaVelo learns a functional form of the vector field, such that the model can be perturbed in silico and not only used to draw trajectories. We show that DynaVelo recovers the bifurcating in vivo dynamics of wild-type murine germinal center (GC) B cells and reveals how these dynamics change under heterozygous loss of epigenetic regulators Arid1a and Ctcf. In silico perturbation yields dynamic and cell-state-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) that recover known TF-to-gene edges in the wild-type GC GRN and predicts those that are disrupted in mutants. Perturbing Arid1aHet GCs in silico identified Ctcf, Stat3 and Bcl6 as rescue targets for Arid1a loss. In vivo experiments in double-heterozygous mice confirmed rescue of the Arid1aHet dark-zone phenotype in all three cases, and multiome profiling of Arid1aHet;CtcfHet GCs validated the predicted shift toward wild-type dynamics.
10.1038/s41587-026-03348-1.summary: Here we present DynaVelo, a generative neural ordinary differential equation model that learns the joint dynamics of gene expression and transcription factor (TF) motif activity from single-cell multiome data.
10.1038/s41587-026-03348-1.title: Deep dynamical models of single-cell multiomic velocities predict loss-of-function and rescue perturbations in B cells

10.1038/s41587-026-03359-y.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.
10.1038/s41587-026-03359-y.summary: Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain.
10.1038/s41587-026-03359-y.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing

10.1038/s41587-026-03360-5.abstract: Microorganisms have the potential to deliver growth-promoting benefits to plants and crops; however, to be useful in a field setting, their gene expression should be programmable and restricted to specific plant hosts and conditions. Here, using O-methyl-L-tyrosine (OMY) as a model compound, we establish noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) as a tool for plant-based control of associated microbial activity. We use genetic code expansion to engineer OMY-dependent control of protein synthesis in the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis. Engineered B. subtilis strains express an orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and tRNA pair that, upon provision of OMY, results in suppression of in-frame amber stop codons in target transcripts. We engineer Arabidopsis, tomato and poplar to biosynthesize OMY, showing that plant-derived OMY can stimulate gene expression in both model and wild soil bacteria. This demonstrates that inducible and tissue-specific expression of a single biosynthetic enzyme by the plant enables on-demand control over microbial activity, establishing ncAAs as a tool for programming plant-microorganism partnerships.
10.1038/s41587-026-03360-5.summary: This demonstrates that inducible and tissue-specific expression of a single biosynthetic enzyme by the plant enables on-demand control over microbial activity, establishing ncAAs as a tool for programming plant-microorganism partnerships.
10.1038/s41587-026-03360-5.title: Genetic code expansion enables plant-directed control of bacterial activity

10.1038/s41592-026-03245-0.abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.
10.1038/s41592-026-03245-0.summary: Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains…
10.1038/s41592-026-03245-0.title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy

10.1038/s41592-026-03252-1.abstract: The dynamic choreography of biomolecular interactions underpins the processes of life, but its direct observation remains challenging. Here we introduce continuous mass photometry, enabling hour-long, mass-resolved observation of individual biomolecules tethered to supported lipid bilayers, their complexes and interactions, with up to sub-kilodalton mass precision and millisecond temporal resolution. Our approach represents a quantitative time-resolved single-molecule measurement modality for studying complex biomolecular mechanisms in action.
10.1038/s41592-026-03252-1.summary: Here we introduce continuous mass photometry, enabling hour-long, mass-resolved observation of individual biomolecules tethered to supported lipid bilayers, their complexes and interactions, with up to sub-kilodalton mass precision and millisecond temporal resolution.
10.1038/s41592-026-03252-1.title: Continuous mass photometry by single-molecule trapping

10.1038/s41592-026-03262-z.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.
10.1038/s41592-026-03262-z.summary: Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP.
10.1038/s41592-026-03262-z.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics

10.1038/s41592-026-03264-x.abstract: Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage-fusion-bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.
10.1038/s41592-026-03264-x.summary: Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage-fusion-bridges and other amplification modes.
10.1038/s41592-026-03264-x.title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes

10.1038/s41592-026-03272-x.abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.
10.1038/s41592-026-03272-x.summary: Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types.
10.1038/s41592-026-03272-x.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics

10.1038/s41592-026-03274-9.abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems.
10.1038/s41592-026-03274-9.summary: Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers.
10.1038/s41592-026-03274-9.title: CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition

10.1056/nejmoa2506756.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthopedic infection is usually managed with surgery and prolonged systemic antibiotic therapy. Whether local antibiotics delivered by a product implanted at the infection site during surgery can reduce the duration of systemic antibiotic therapy is unclear.

METHODS: In a multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned, in a 1:1 ratio, adults who had undergone surgery for orthopedic infection and implantation of a local-antibiotic carrier to receive postoperative systemic antibiotic therapy for a long (≥4 weeks) or short (≤7 days) duration. The primary outcome was definite treatment failure by 12 months, assessed according to protocol-defined criteria by a clinical end-point committee whose members were unaware of the trial-group assignments. The noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points.

RESULTS: A total of 500 patients underwent randomization, of whom 475 were assessed in the primary analysis. Definite treatment failure occurred in 34 of 241 patients (14.1%) in the long-duration group and in 26 of 234 patients (11.1%) in the short-duration group (risk difference [negative values favor the short duration], -3.0 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -9.0 to 3.0), which met the prespecified noninferiority margin. In sensitivity analyses in the included population (497 patients) and the per-protocol population (457 patients), results were consistent with those of the primary analysis (risk difference, -2.4 percentage points [95% CI, -8.2 to 3.5] and -2.7 percentage points [95% CI, -8.8 to 3.4], respectively). By week 6 after surgery, symptoms potentially related to treatment had occurred in 45.2% of the patients in the long-duration group and in 17.2% of those in the short-duration group (risk difference, -28.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -36.4 to -19.6).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who had undergone orthopedic surgery and received local antibiotics, a short course of systemic antibiotics was noninferior to a long course with respect to definite treatment failure by 12 months. (Funded by the European Bone and Joint Infection Society and others; SOLARIO ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03806166.).

10.1056/nejmoa2601088.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sjögren's disease is a complex, systemic autoimmune disease with no approved targeted therapies. Ianalumab is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody with a dual mechanism of action, depleting B cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and inhibiting B-cell activation and survival through blockade of B-cell activating factor receptor.

METHODS: We conducted two 52-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease. Patients in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ianalumab (300 mg monthly) or placebo; patients in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial were assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive 300 mg of ianalumab monthly or every 3 months or placebo. The primary end point was the change from baseline in the score on the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) at week 48 (scores range from 0 to 123, with higher scores indicating greater disease activity). The first key secondary end point in the hierarchical plan for the NEPTUNUS-1 trial was an ESSDAI response (≥5-point reduction) at week 48; for the NEPTUNUS-2 trial, it was the change from baseline in the score on the Sjögren's Syndrome Symptom Diary (SSSD) or EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI) at week 48.

RESULTS: Overall, 275 patients underwent randomization in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial (ianalumab monthly, 137 patients; placebo, 138 patients) and 504 in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial (ianalumab monthly, 168 patients; ianalumab every 3 months, 167 patients; and placebo, 169 patients). In both trials, ianalumab monthly led to a significantly greater decrease in the ESSDAI score at week 48 than placebo, with a between-group difference of -1.3 points (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.6 to 0.0; P = 0.0496) in NEPTUNUS-1 and -1.0 points (95% CI, -2.0 to 0.0; P = 0.04) in NEPTUNUS-2. No significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI scores were observed at week 48. The incidence of serious adverse events was similar with ianalumab and placebo. Nonserious local injection-site and systemic injection-related reactions were more common in the ianalumab groups.

CONCLUSIONS: In these two trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease, ianalumab at a dose of 300 mg monthly resulted in a significantly greater decrease in disease activity at week 48 than placebo, although there were no significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI symptom scores. (Funded by Novartis Pharma; NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05350072 and NCT05349214, respectively.).

10.1056/nejmoa2601088.title: Ianalumab for the Treatment of Patients with Sjögren’s Disease

10.1056/nejmoa2603021.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a common condition that is associated with substantial morbidity and no proven medical therapy. Whether treatment with aficamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor, can benefit patients with this condition is unknown.

METHODS: In this phase 3, multinational, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned adults with symptomatic nonobstructive HCM in a 1:1 ratio to receive aficamten (starting dose, 5 mg; maximum dose, 20 mg) or placebo for up to 72 weeks. The dual primary end points were the change from baseline to week 36 in peak oxygen uptake and in the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire clinical summary score (KCCQ-CSS; range, 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better health status).

RESULTS: A total of 258 patients were assigned to receive aficamten and 259 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 55.1 years, and 53.6% were women. At 36 weeks, the change in the KCCQ-CSS was 11.4 points (95% confidence interval [CI], 9.6 to 13.2) in the aficamten group and 8.4 points (95% CI, 6.6 to 10.2) in the placebo group (least-squares mean difference, 3.0 points; 95% CI, 0.5 to 5.5; P = 0.02). The mean change in the peak oxygen uptake at week 36 was 0.64 ml per kilogram of body weight per minute (95% CI, 0.32 to 0.95) in the aficamten group and -0.03 ml per kilogram per minute (95% CI, -0.35 to 0.28) in the placebo group (least-squares mean difference, 0.67 ml per kilogram per minute; 95% CI, 0.22 to 1.11; P = 0.003). Reversible reductions in left ventricular ejection fraction to less than 50% occurred in 27 patients (10.5%) receiving aficamten and in 2 patients (0.8%) receiving placebo. Serious adverse events occurred in 52 patients (20.2%) and 38 patients (14.7%), respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with symptomatic nonobstructive HCM, treatment with aficamten resulted in a significantly greater change in exercise capacity and patient-reported health status than placebo at 36 weeks. (Funded by Cytokinetics; ACACIA-HCM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06081894.).
10.1056/nejmoa2603021.summary: Among patients with symptomatic nonobstructive HCM, treatment with aficamten resulted in a significantly greater change in exercise capacity and patient-reported health status than placebo at 36 weeks.
10.1056/nejmoa2603021.title: Aficamten for Symptomatic Nonobstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

10.1056/nejmoa2603649.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aspirin after an initial short course of rivaroxaban has been shown to be safe and effective for the prevention of venous thromboembolism after total hip or total knee arthroplasty, but uncertainty remains about the use of aspirin alone.

METHODS: In this multicenter, double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, we assigned patients to receive once-daily thromboprophylaxis with either 81 mg of aspirin or 10 mg of oral rivaroxaban for the first 5 days after total hip or total knee arthroplasty. All the patients then received further thromboprophylaxis with 81 mg of aspirin daily for 9 additional days after knee arthroplasty and for 30 additional days after hip arthroplasty. Patients were followed for 90 days for symptomatic venous thromboembolism, which consisted of either proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism (primary effectiveness outcome), and for bleeding complications (primary safety outcome). The noninferiority margin for aspirin alone as compared with rivaroxaban-aspirin was 0.7 percentage points.

RESULTS: A total of 5429 patients underwent randomization. Venous thromboembolism developed in 13 of 2718 patients (0.48%) in the aspirin-alone group and in 12 of 2647 patients (0.45%) in the rivaroxaban-aspirin group (risk difference, 0.02 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.34 to 0.39; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Major bleeding or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding events occurred in 45 of 2718 patients (1.66%) in the aspirin-alone group and in 54 of 2647 patients (2.04%) in the rivaroxaban-aspirin group (risk difference, -0.38%; 95% CI, -1.11 to 0.34).

CONCLUSIONS: After total hip and total knee arthroplasty, the use of aspirin alone was not inferior to a strategy of using rivaroxaban followed by aspirin for the prevention of symptomatic venous thromboembolism, with no clinically relevant difference in bleeding events. (Funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; EPCAT III ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04075240.).
10.1056/nejmoa2603649.summary: After total hip and total knee arthroplasty, the use of aspirin alone was not inferior to a strategy of using rivaroxaban followed by aspirin for the prevention of symptomatic venous thromboembolism, with no clinically relevant difference in bleeding events.
10.1056/nejmoa2603649.title: Rivaroxaban Then Aspirin vs. Aspirin Alone after Total Hip or Knee Arthroplasty

10.1056/nejmoa2604169.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Retatrutide is a triple-receptor agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide-1, and glucagon receptors.

METHODS: In this phase 3, randomized, double-blind trial, we assigned adults with obesity without diabetes to receive a once-weekly subcutaneous injection of retatrutide (at a dose of 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg) or placebo for 80 weeks. Primary outcomes (evaluated in the 9-mg and 12-mg groups each vs. placebo) were the percent change in body weight and the change in the WOMAC pain score (ranging from 1 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) in the subgroup of 574 participants with knee osteoarthritis and the change in the apnea-hypopnea index in the 243 participants with obstructive sleep apnea. For weight-related end points, intercurrent events were handled by a treatment-regimen estimand (intention-to-treat [ITT]). For end points in participants with knee osteoarthritis or obstructive sleep apnea, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy for intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure; ITT results are also reported.

RESULTS: A total of 2339 participants underwent randomization. The mean percent change in body weight in the retatrutide groups was -17.6% (4-mg dose), -23.7% (9-mg dose), and -25.0% (12-mg dose) versus -3.9% in the placebo group (differences, -19.8 and -21.0 percentage points, respectively; P<0.001 for both comparisons). Among the participants with knee osteoarthritis, the corresponding changes in the pain score in the retatrutide groups for the hybrid estimand were -3.2, -3.5, and -3.6 versus -1.9 with placebo (differences, -1.6 and -1.8 points; both P<0.001); the corresponding changes for the ITT estimand were -3.4, -3.9, and -4.1 versus -2.5 with placebo (differences, -1.4 and -1.6 points; both P<0.001). Among the participants with obstructive sleep apnea, the corresponding changes in events per hour in the retatrutide groups for the hybrid-treatment estimand were -22.9, -34.3, and 31.7 versus -9.9 (differences, -24.4 and -21.9; both P<0.001); the corresponding changes for the ITT estimand were -22.8, -34.3, and -32.1 versus -9.6 (differences, -24.7 and -22.5; both P<0.001). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.

CONCLUSIONS: In adults with obesity, retatrutide resulted in significant weight reduction, reduced pain in participants with knee osteoarthritis, and reduced apnea-hypopnea events in participants with obstructive sleep apnea. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05929066.).
10.1056/nejmoa2604169.summary: In adults with obesity, retatrutide resulted in significant weight reduction, reduced pain in participants with knee osteoarthritis, and reduced apnea-hypopnea events in participants with obstructive sleep apnea.
10.1056/nejmoa2604169.title: Retatrutide, a Triple Hormone Receptor Agonist, for Treatment of Obesity

10.1056/nejmoa2605703.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Divarasib, a next-generation, oral KRAS G12C inhibitor, is more potent and selective in vitro than the first-generation KRAS G12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib.

METHODS: In this phase 3, international, open-label trial, patients with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated advanced or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) were randomly assigned to receive divarasib orally at a dose of 400 mg once daily or control treatment (sotorasib orally at a dose of 960 mg once daily or adagrasib orally at a dose of 600 mg twice daily) until the occurrence of disease progression, unacceptable adverse events, loss of clinical benefit, withdrawal of consent, death, or trial termination. The primary end point was progression-free survival as assessed by blinded independent central review. Secondary end points included overall survival, confirmed overall response, duration of response, patient-reported outcomes, and safety.

RESULTS: A total of 338 patients received divarasib (167 patients) or control treatment (171 patients; 156 received sotorasib and 15 received adagrasib). The median follow-up was 14.3 months. The median progression-free survival was 9.8 months with divarasib and 5.7 months with control treatment (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.58; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.44 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median overall survival was 17.7 months with divarasib and 12.0 months with control treatment (hazard ratio for death, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.78; P<0.001). Of the 328 patients who could be evaluated for response, a confirmed response occurred in 58.4% in the divarasib group and in 32.3% in the control group. The median duration of response was 11.9 months with divarasib and 6.9 months with control treatment. Fewer grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events were noted with divarasib (24.6%) than with control treatment (34.5%).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated advanced or metastatic NSCLC, divarasib led to significantly longer progression-free and overall survival than control treatment. (Supported by F. Hoffmann-La Roche; Krascendo 1 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06497556.).
10.1056/nejmoa2605703.summary: Among patients with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated advanced or metastatic NSCLC, divarasib led to significantly longer progression-free and overall survival than control treatment.
10.1056/nejmoa2605703.title: Divarasib as Compared with Sotorasib or Adagrasib in KRAS G12C–Mutated NSCLC

10.1056/nejmoa2605812.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with syncope who present to the emergency department for evaluation, diagnosing an underlying cardiac arrhythmia remains difficult.

METHODS: We conducted an open-label, randomized, controlled trial at 45 hospitals in the United Kingdom to assess the effects of 14-day cardiac monitoring on diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes among patients with syncope. Adults with syncope that remained unexplained after an evaluation in the emergency department were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo 14-day ambulatory electrocardiographic (ECG) monitoring (the intervention group) or to receive the standard care provided for patients with unexplained syncope at each participating site (the standard-care group). The primary outcome was the mean number of patient-reported episodes of syncope at 1 year.

RESULTS: A total of 2234 patients underwent randomization: 1123 were assigned to the intervention group and 1111 to the standard-care group. The mean age of the patients was 58.3 years, and 52.1% were male. After the exclusion of patients who did not complete any follow-up, a total of 1970 patients (1004 in the intervention group and 966 in the standard-care group) were included in the primary analysis. The mean (±SD) number of patient-reported syncope episodes at 1 year was 1.37±5.10 in the intervention group and 1.58±8.56 in the standard-care group (incidence rate ratio, 0.89; 95% confidence interval, 0.68 to 1.18; P = 0.42). A total of 49 adverse events were reported in the intervention group, and 8 adverse events were reported in the standard-care group, with 1 serious adverse event in each group.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with syncope that remained unexplained after evaluation in the emergency department, the use of 14-day ambulatory ECG monitoring did not result in significantly fewer patient-reported syncope episodes at 1 year than standard care. (Funded by the British Heart Foundation and National Health Service Research Scotland; ASPIRED ISRCTN Registry number, ISRCTN10278811.).
10.1056/nejmoa2605812.summary: Among patients with syncope that remained unexplained after evaluation in the emergency department, the use of 14-day ambulatory ECG monitoring did not result in significantly fewer patient-reported syncope episodes at 1 year than standard care.
10.1056/nejmoa2605812.title: Immediate Ambulatory Electrocardiographic Monitoring in Syncope

10.1056/nejmoa2606924.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Approximately one half of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic-valve implantation (TAVI) have concomitant coronary artery disease. Although percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is often performed before TAVI, the preferred treatment strategy has not been established.

METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial at 48 centers in Europe. Patients with severe aortic stenosis and coronary artery disease were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to a strategy of either TAVI before PCI (TAVI-first group) or PCI before TAVI (PCI-first group). The primary end point was a composite of death from any cause; nonfatal myocardial infarction; ischemia-driven revascularization; rehospitalization related to the valve, procedure, or heart failure; or life-threatening, disabling, or major bleeding at 1 year after randomization. The noninferiority margin was 6.6 percentage points, with testing for noninferiority of TAVI first as compared with PCI first.

RESULTS: A total of 986 patients underwent randomization: 498 were assigned to the TAVI-first group and 488 to the PCI-first group. A primary end-point event occurred in 105 patients (22.2%) in the TAVI-first group and in 112 patients (24.2%) in the PCI-first group (risk difference, -2.0 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -7.4 to 3.4; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Serious adverse events occurred in 264 patients in the TAVI-first group and in 273 patients in the PCI-first group.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with severe aortic stenosis and coronary artery disease, a strategy of TAVI before PCI was noninferior to a strategy of PCI before TAVI with respect to the primary end point at 1 year. (Funded by University Hospital Zurich and others; TAVI PCI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04310046.).
10.1056/nejmoa2606924.summary: Among patients with severe aortic stenosis and coronary artery disease, a strategy of TAVI before PCI was noninferior to a strategy of PCI before TAVI with respect to the primary end point at 1 year.
10.1056/nejmoa2606924.title: Timing of PCI in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Implantation

10.1056/nejmoa2606997.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The safety of omitting up-front treatment with aspirin during primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains unclear.

METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial in Japan involving patients with STEMI who were undergoing primary PCI. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio before PCI to receive low-dose prasugrel monotherapy or dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and low-dose prasugrel for 12 months. The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, stroke, or myocardial infarction at 12 months, which was assessed for noninferiority with a prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.50 for the 95% confidence interval of the hazard ratio. The major secondary outcome was major bleeding (defined as a bleeding event of Bleeding Academic Research Consortium [BARC] type 3 [nonfatal major bleeding] or 5 [fatal bleeding]) at 12 months, which was assessed for superiority if noninferiority was established for the primary outcome.

RESULTS: A total of 2216 patients were included in the full analysis population; 1109 were assigned to receive monotherapy and 1107 to receive DAPT. At 12 months, death from any cause, stroke, or myocardial infarction had occurred in 124 patients (Kaplan-Meier estimate, 11.0%) in the monotherapy group and in 94 patients (Kaplan-Meier estimate, 8.5%) in the DAPT group (hazard ratio, 1.34; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02 to 1.75; P = 0.40 for noninferiority). Major bleeding had occurred in 61 patients (Kaplan-Meier estimate, 5.6%) in the monotherapy group and in 92 patients (Kaplan-Meier estimate, 8.4%) in the DAPT group (hazard ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.91). The percentages of patients with definite or probable stent thrombosis and serious adverse events appeared to be similar in the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with STEMI who were undergoing primary PCI, low-dose prasugrel monotherapy initiated before PCI was not noninferior to DAPT for 12 months with respect to a composite of death from any cause, stroke, or myocardial infarction at 12 months. (Funded by Boston Scientific Japan; PREMIUM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05709626.).
10.1056/nejmoa2606997.summary: Among patients with STEMI who were undergoing primary PCI, low-dose prasugrel monotherapy initiated before PCI was not noninferior to DAPT for 12 months with respect to a composite of death from any cause, stroke, or myocardial infarction at 12 months.
10.1056/nejmoa2606997.title: Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in STEMI

10.1056/nejmoa2606998.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Many patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have exacerbations despite receiving standard-of-care inhaled maintenance therapy. Dysregulated interleukin-33 signaling is implicated in the pathogenesis of COPD. Tozorakimab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the activity of interleukin-33.

METHODS: In two replicate phase 3 trials (OBERON and TITANIA), we enrolled adults with COPD who were current or former smokers and had a history of exacerbations in the previous year despite receiving stable standard-of-care inhaled maintenance therapy. There were no eligibility criteria related to blood eosinophil count. Patients were randomly assigned to receive add-on subcutaneous tozorakimab (300 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. The primary end point was the annualized rate of moderate or severe exacerbations that occurred over a 52-week period among former smokers, and the first key secondary end point was the annualized rate of moderate or severe exacerbations in the overall population. Safety was also assessed.

RESULTS: The overall population in OBERON included 446 patients in the tozorakimab group and 431 in the placebo group, and in TITANIA included 438 in the tozorakimab group and 435 in the placebo group. The annualized rate of moderate or severe exacerbations among former smokers was 1.34 events in the tozorakimab group and 1.90 events in the placebo group (rate ratio, 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.88; P = 0.002) in OBERON, and 1.37 events and 2.07 events, respectively (rate ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.55 to 0.80; P<0.001), in TITANIA. In the overall population, the annualized rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 1.41 events in the tozorakimab group and 2.00 events in the placebo group (rate ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.58 to 0.85; P<0.001) in OBERON, and 1.44 events and 2.03 events, respectively (rate ratio, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.84; P<0.001), in TITANIA. Adverse events occurred in 70.4% of the patients in the tozorakimab group and in 77.2% of those in the placebo group in OBERON, and in 80.1% and 79.8%, respectively, in TITANIA.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with COPD, treatment with tozorakimab resulted in a significantly lower rate of moderate or severe exacerbations than placebo in the cohort of former smokers and in the overall population of current and former smokers. (Funded by AstraZeneca; OBERON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05166889; TITANIA ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05158387.).
10.1056/nejmoa2606998.summary: Among patients with COPD, treatment with tozorakimab resulted in a significantly lower rate of moderate or severe exacerbations than placebo in the cohort of former smokers and in the overall population of current and former smokers.
10.1056/nejmoa2606998.title: Tozorakimab to Prevent COPD Exacerbations

10.1056/nejmoa2607219.abstract:
BACKGROUND: For persons living with both type 2 diabetes and obesity, weight management may be the most effective therapy for type 2 diabetes. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have potent weight-reducing effects, and other mechanisms may confer additional benefits. Survodutide is an investigational glucagon receptor-GLP-1 receptor dual agonist with potential weight-reducing and metabolic benefits.

METHODS: In this multinational, double-blind, phase 3 trial involving adults with type 2 diabetes and a body-mass index (BMI; the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of 27 or more, we randomly assigned participants in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (3.6 mg or 6.0 mg) or placebo. The two primary end points were the percent change in body weight and a reduction in body weight of at least 5% from baseline to week 76.

RESULTS: Among 752 participants (250 in the 3.6-mg survodutide group, 251 in the 6.0-mg survodutide group, and 251 in the placebo group), the mean age at baseline was 55.7 years, and the mean BMI was 36.5; 49.3% were men. The mean weight change at week 76 according to the treatment-regimen estimand (which assessed effects regardless of whether the trial regimen was discontinued or interrupted or whether other antiobesity therapies were used) was -8.2% (95% confidence interval [CI], -9.2 to -7.2) in the 3.6-mg group, -9.8% (95% CI, -10.8 to -8.8) in the 6.0-mg group, and -3.9% (95% CI, -4.9 to -2.9) in the placebo group; weight reduction of at least 5% occurred in 57.6%, 64.5%, and 35.1% of the participants, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The mean change in the glycated hemoglobin level (from a baseline level of 7.4%) was -0.9 percentage points in the 3.6-mg group, -0.8 percentage points in the 6.0-mg group, and -0.2 percentage points in the placebo group. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal (generally mild to moderate and transient), which occurred in 182 participants (72.8%) in the 3.6-mg group, 195 (77.7%) in the 6.0-mg group, and 97 (38.6%) in the placebo group.

CONCLUSIONS: In adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, survodutide at a weekly dose of 3.6 mg or 6.0 mg resulted in significantly greater weight reduction than placebo. (Funded by Boehringer Ingelheim; SYNCHRONIZE-2 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06066528.).
10.1056/nejmoa2607219.summary: In adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, survodutide at a weekly dose of 3.6 mg or 6.0 mg resulted in significantly greater weight reduction than placebo.
10.1056/nejmoa2607219.title: Survodutide Once Weekly in Adults with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes

10.1056/nejmoa2607544.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with IgA nephropathy, complement activation drives glomerular inflammation, which leads to hematuria, proteinuria, and nephron loss. Ravulizumab is a terminal complement inhibitor that prevents formation of C5a and C5b-9.

METHODS: In this phase 3 trial, we enrolled adults with IgA nephropathy who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 30 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and proteinuria (24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio [with protein and creatinine both measured in grams] of ≥0.75 or total urinary protein excretion of ≥1.0 g per day), despite standard therapy. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive an intravenous infusion of either ravulizumab or placebo every 8 weeks. In the prespecified interim analysis, the primary efficacy end point was the change from baseline in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 34. Safety was also assessed.

RESULTS: In all, 485 patients underwent randomization, with 240 patients assigned to the ravulizumab group and 245 to the placebo group; 352 patients (176 in each group) were included in the interim analysis. In the ravulizumab group, the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at baseline and at week 34 was 1.56 and 0.83, respectively; in the placebo group, it was 1.60 and 1.48, respectively. At week 34, a significant reduction in the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was observed with ravulizumab (-46.6%) as compared with the reduction observed with placebo (-5.6%), corresponding to an adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio that was 43.4% (99% confidence interval, 30.1 to 54.2) lower with ravulizumab than with placebo (P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 69.5% of the patients receiving ravulizumab and in 75.8% of those receiving placebo; serious adverse events occurred in 4.6% and 9.0%, respectively. No meningococcal infections or deaths occurred.

CONCLUSIONS: In adults with IgA nephropathy, ravulizumab resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo at week 34. (Funded by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease Unit; I CAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06291376; EU Clinical Trials number, 2023-507851-31-00.).
10.1056/nejmoa2607544.summary: In adults with IgA nephropathy, ravulizumab resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo at week 34.
10.1056/nejmoa2607544.title: Ravulizumab in IgA Nephropathy — Interim Analysis of a Phase 3 Trial

10.1056/nejmoa2607887.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with infective endocarditis on the left side of the heart, the current recommendation of up to 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy is based largely on expert consensus opinion. Whether a clinical response-tailored antibiotic management strategy can shorten treatment duration without compromising safety is unclear.

METHODS: In this international, open-label, randomized trial, we assigned adults in stable condition with infective endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus faecalis, or streptococcus species to receive either response-tailored or standard-duration antibiotic therapy. Before randomization, all the patients received at least the prespecified 2 to 4 weeks of therapy and met criteria for clinical stabilization. After randomization, patients in the tailored-therapy group discontinued antibiotics and those in the standard-therapy group continued standard treatment (total duration, 4 to 6 weeks). The primary efficacy end point was days alive without antibiotic treatment for infective endocarditis or bacteremia within 6 months after randomization (tested for superiority). The primary safety end point was a composite of death from any cause, unplanned cardiac surgery, or symptomatic embolic events within 6 months after randomization (tested for noninferiority; margin, 7.5 percentage points). Relapse of bacteremia or infective endocarditis was a key secondary end point.

RESULTS: A total of 508 patients underwent randomization, with 255 assigned to response-tailored therapy and 253 to standard-duration therapy. The median time alive without antibiotic treatment was 183 days (interquartile range, 181 to 183) with tailored therapy and 169 days (interquartile range, 166 to 171) with standard therapy (Hodges-Lehmann estimated difference, 13 days; 95% confidence interval [CI], 12 to 13; P<0.001 for superiority). A primary safety end-point event occurred in 21 patients (8.2%) with tailored therapy and in 27 patients (10.7%) with standard therapy (absolute between-group difference, -2.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -7.7 to 2.7; P<0.001 for noninferiority), indicating noninferiority. Relapse occurred in 13 patients (5.1%) with tailored therapy and in 4 patients (1.6%) with standard therapy (P = 0.04).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with infective endocarditis on the left side of the heart, the use of a response-tailored antibiotic strategy resulted in a longer time alive without antibiotic therapy than standard-duration therapy and met the criterion for noninferiority with respect to safety but was associated with a higher incidence of relapse of bacteremia or infective endocarditis. (Funded by Sygeforsikringen "danmark" and others; POET II ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03851575.).

10.1056/nejmoa2607887.title: Response-Tailored or Standard-Duration Antibiotic Treatment for Infective Endocarditis

10.1056/nejmoa2608012.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether catheter-directed thrombolysis improves clinical outcomes in patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism, as compared with anticoagulation alone, is uncertain.

METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial, we randomly assigned patients with intermediate-high-risk acute pulmonary embolism (defined by hemodynamic stability, a simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index score of ≥1, and right ventricular dysfunction plus an elevated level of cardiac troponin or natriuretic peptide) in a 1:1 ratio to receive catheter-directed thrombolysis with alteplase plus anticoagulation therapy (thrombolysis group) or anticoagulation therapy alone (standard-care group). The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, recurrence of pulmonary embolism, or cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse within 7 days after randomization. Secondary outcomes included clinically relevant bleeding as defined by the Bleeding Academic Research Consortium, major bleeding as defined in the Global Use of Strategies to Open Occluded Coronary Arteries guidelines, and intracranial hemorrhage.

RESULTS: A total of 558 patients underwent randomization; 280 were assigned to the thrombolysis group, and 278 to the standard-care group. The median age was 64 years, and 40.9% were female. A primary-outcome event occurred in 2 patients (0.7%) in the thrombolysis group and in 19 patients (6.8%) in the standard-care group (relative risk, 0.10; 95% confidence interval, 0.02 to 0.44; P<0.001); this difference was driven mainly by the lower incidence of cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse in the thrombolysis group. By day 7, clinically relevant bleeding had occurred in 13 patients (4.6%) in the thrombolysis group and in 14 patients (5.0%) in the standard-care group (P = 0.85); major bleeding in 4 (1.4%) and 6 (2.2%), respectively (P = 0.54); and intracranial hemorrhage in 2 (0.7%) and none. One patient in the thrombolysis group died within 30 days, and 4 patients in the standard-care group died within 7 days.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with intermediate-high-risk acute pulmonary embolism, catheter-directed thrombolysis with alteplase plus anticoagulation therapy led to a lower risk of death from any cause, recurrent pulmonary embolism, or cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse within 7 days after randomization than anticoagulation therapy alone. (Funded by the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic and others; PRAGUE-26 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05493163; EudraCT number, 2022-002218-18; European Union Clinical Trials number, 2024-516144-25-00.).

10.1056/nejmoa2608012.title: Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis in Intermediate-High–Risk Pulmonary Embolism

BACKGROUND: The standard of care for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer continues to evolve. Whether perioperative durvalumab, with or without tremelimumab, plus neoadjuvant enfortumab vedotin is effective in such patients is unknown.

METHODS: In this phase 3 open-label trial, we randomly assigned, in a 1:1:1 ratio, patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer who were ineligible for or declined cisplatin-based chemotherapy to receive neoadjuvant durvalumab-enfortumab vedotin every 3 weeks for three cycles, followed by radical cystectomy and then adjuvant durvalumab every 4 weeks for nine cycles; neoadjuvant durvalumab-tremelimumab-enfortumab vedotin (tremelimumab for two cycles only), radical cystectomy, and adjuvant durvalumab-tremelimumab (tremelimumab for one cycle only); or radical cystectomy alone (control). The dual primary end points were event-free survival in each of the two durvalumab groups as compared with that in the control group. The two durvalumab groups were not compared with each other. The key secondary end point was overall survival.

RESULTS: In total, 233 patients were assigned to the durvalumab-enfortumab vedotin group, 233 to the durvalumab-tremelimumab-enfortumab vedotin group, and 229 to the control group. Estimated event-free survival at 24 months was 63.5% (95% confidence interval [CI], 56.5 to 69.7) with durvalumab-enfortumab vedotin and 45.1% (95% CI, 38.2 to 51.8) with control (hazard ratio for an event or death, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38 to 0.67; P<0.001); estimated overall survival at 24 months was 78.4% and 69.4%, respectively (hazard ratio for death, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.83; P = 0.003). Estimated event-free survival at 24 months was 60.1% (95% CI, 53.2 to 66.2) with durvalumab-tremelimumab-enfortumab vedotin (hazard ratio for an event or death vs. control, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.80; P<0.001). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 71.1% of patients in the durvalumab-enfortumab vedotin group (treatment-related, 30.7%), in 79.5% of those in the durvalumab-tremelimumab-enfortumab vedotin group (treatment-related, 44.5%), and in 50.2% of those in the control group.

CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative durvalumab with or without tremelimumab plus three cycles of neoadjuvant enfortumab vedotin resulted in significantly better event-free survival outcomes than surgery alone. Perioperative durvalumab plus enfortumab vedotin led to significantly better overall survival outcomes than surgery alone. Grade 3 or higher adverse events of any cause were noted in more than half the patients in the durvalumab groups. (Funded by AstraZeneca; VOLGA ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04960709; EudraCT number, 2020-005452-38.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608323.summary: Perioperative durvalumab with or without tremelimumab plus three cycles of neoadjuvant enfortumab vedotin resulted in significantly better event-free survival outcomes than surgery alone.
10.1056/nejmoa2608323.title: Durvalumab, Tremelimumab, and Enfortumab Vedotin in Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer

BACKGROUND: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain.

METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90.

RESULTS: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group.

CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).
