10.1056/nejmoa2608510.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transthyretin amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a progressive, life-threatening disease caused by deposition of misfolded transthyretin (TTR). Eplontersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces the production of hepatic TTR. The effect of eplontersen on ATTR-CM is unclear.

METHODS: In this phase 3, international, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned, in a 1:1 ratio, patients with ATTR-CM to receive subcutaneous eplontersen (45 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks for 140 weeks, in addition to standard treatment. The primary end point was a cumulative composite of death from cardiovascular causes and recurrent cardiovascular clinical events up to week 140. The effect of death from noncardiovascular causes on the primary analysis was assessed with a cumulative composite of death from any cause and cardiovascular events up to week 140.

RESULTS: A total of 1432 patients underwent randomization and received at least one dose of the assigned intervention (715 patients in the eplontersen group and 717 in the placebo group). The mean age of the patients was 76.4 years, and 90.6% were men. A total of 381 primary end-point events occurred in 210 patients (29.4%) receiving eplontersen, and 392 events occurred in 231 patients (32.2%) receiving placebo (rate ratio, 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 1.09; P = 0.28). Death from cardiovascular causes, as a component of the primary end point, occurred in 74 patients in the eplontersen group and in 70 in the placebo group; there were 307 cardiovascular clinical events in the eplontersen group and 322 in the placebo group. The rate ratio for the composite of death from any cause and cardiovascular events was 0.86 (95% CI, 0.71 to 1.04). Serious adverse events occurred in 413 patients (57.8%) in the eplontersen group and in 426 (59.4%) in the placebo group.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with ATTR-CM, eplontersen therapy did not lead to a lower risk of a composite of death from cardiovascular causes and recurrent cardiovascular events than placebo up to 140 weeks. (Funded by Ionis Pharmaceuticals and AstraZeneca; CARDIO-TTRansform ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04136171.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608510.summary: Among patients with ATTR-CM, eplontersen therapy did not lead to a lower risk of a composite of death from cardiovascular causes and recurrent cardiovascular events than placebo up to 140 weeks.
10.1056/nejmoa2608510.title: Eplontersen for Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy

10.1056/nejmoa2608533.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effect of clopidogrel monotherapy as compared with extended dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with clopidogrel and aspirin beyond 12 months after implantation of a drug-eluting stent remains uncertain in patients at high risk for recurrent ischemic events.

METHODS: In this open-label noninferiority trial conducted in South Korea, we enrolled patients with high-risk clinical or lesion characteristics in whom a drug-eluting stent had been implanted 12 months earlier and randomly assigned them, in a 1:1 ratio, to receive clopidogrel monotherapy or extended DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin). The primary end point was net adverse clinical events, a composite of death from any cause, myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, stroke, or Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 2, 3, or 5 bleeding at 24 months (noninferiority margin, 2.3 percentage points). Key secondary ischemic and bleeding end points were tested in a prespecified hierarchical order.

RESULTS: Of the 3203 patients who underwent randomization, 1601 were assigned to receive clopidogrel monotherapy and 1602 to receive extended DAPT. Over the course of 24 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 80 patients (5.0%) in the monotherapy group and in 81 (5.1%) in the DAPT group (risk difference, -0.1 percentage points; 90% confidence interval [CI], -1.3 to 1.2; P = 0.001 for noninferiority). Death from any cause, myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, or stroke (the key secondary ischemic end point) occurred in 60 patients (3.7%) in the monotherapy group and in 26 (1.6%) in the DAPT group (hazard ratio, 2.33; 95% CI, 1.47 to 3.69; P<0.001). BARC type 2, 3, or 5 bleeding (the key secondary bleeding end point) occurred in 28 patients (1.8%) in the monotherapy group and in 65 (4.1%) in the DAPT group (hazard ratio, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.67; P<0.001). The incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients at high risk for ischemic events 12 months after drug-eluting stent implantation, clopidogrel monotherapy was noninferior to extended DAPT with respect to net adverse clinical events at 24 months. (Funded by Chong Kun Dang and Samjin; A-CLOSE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03947229.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608533.summary: Among patients at high risk for ischemic events 12 months after drug-eluting stent implantation, clopidogrel monotherapy was noninferior to extended DAPT with respect to net adverse clinical events at 24 months.
10.1056/nejmoa2608533.title: Clopidogrel or Dual Antiplatelet Therapy in High-Ischemic-Risk Patients

10.1056/nejmoa2608571.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study.

METHODS: In a 26-week trial conducted at 22 primary care practices in the United States, we randomly assigned adults with type 2 diabetes who were not using insulin to either CGM or routine care (control). The primary outcome was the glycated hemoglobin level at 26 weeks. Key CGM-measured secondary outcomes were tested hierarchically to control the type I error rate.

RESULTS: A total of 145 participants were assigned to the CGM group, and 138 to the routine-care group. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 84 years. The mean (±SD) glycated hemoglobin level decreased from 8.8±1.3% at baseline to 7.2±1.1% at 26 weeks in the CGM group and from 8.7±1.2% to 8.0±1.4% in the routine-care group (adjusted mean difference, -0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.1 to -0.6; P<0.001). The mean percentage of time that the CGM-measured glucose level was in the glucose-level range of 70 to 180 mg per deciliter was 21 percentage points higher (95% CI, 16 to 26) with CGM than with routine care (P<0.001). The between-group difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 54 mg per deciliter was -0.17 percentage points (95% CI, -0.27 to -0.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority); the difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 70 mg per deciliter was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.004 for superiority). No severe hypoglycemia events were reported.

CONCLUSIONS: Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care. (Funded by Dexcom; CONNECT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06601166.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608571.summary: Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care.
10.1056/nejmoa2608571.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Non–Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes

10.1056/nejmoa2608682.abstract:
BACKGROUND: B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) have distinct roles in IgA-producing B-cell populations and appear to be central to the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy. Povetacicept, an enhanced, variant transmembrane activator and calcium-modulator and cyclophilin-ligand interactor (TACI)-Fc fragment fusion therapeutic, is engineered for dual inhibition of BAFF and APRIL.

METHODS: In this ongoing, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy receiving stable background therapy were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive povetacicept at a dose of 80 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The primary end point of this prespecified interim analysis was the change in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 36. Secondary end points were the change at week 36 in galactose-deficient IgA1 levels and hematuria resolution at week 36 among participants with baseline hematuria.

RESULTS: A total of 557 participants received povetacicept (372 participants) or placebo (185 participants). Efficacy analyses included the first 199 participants who had undergone randomization (131 in the povetacicept group and 68 in the placebo group). The 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased by 52.0% with povetacicept and by 4.3% with placebo by week 36 (adjusted difference, -49.8 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -58.6 to -39.2; P<0.001). Galactose-deficient IgA1 levels decreased by 77.4% with povetacicept and increased by 9.1% with placebo (adjusted difference, -79.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -82.2 to -75.9; P<0.001). Among the participants with baseline hematuria, resolution occurred in 85% with povetacicept and in 23% with placebo (adjusted difference, 62 percentage points; 95% CI, 45 to 78; P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events (75% with povetacicept and 78% with placebo) and serious adverse events (3% and 4%, respectively) were similar in the trial groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Povetacicept led to a significantly greater reduction in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo by week 36 in participants with IgA nephropathy. (Funded by Vertex Pharmaceuticals; RAINIER AIS-D08 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06564142.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608682.summary: Povetacicept led to a significantly greater reduction in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo by week 36 in participants with IgA nephropathy.
10.1056/nejmoa2608682.title: Interim Analysis of a Phase 3 Trial of Povetacicept in IgA Nephropathy

10.1056/nejmoa2608717.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients are at increased risk for recurrent ischemic events after an acute coronary syndrome event. Milvexian, an oral factor XIa inhibitor, may reduce the risk of major adverse clinical events with minimal bleeding risk.

METHODS: In this phase 3, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of milvexian when added to standard antiplatelet therapy within 7 days after an acute coronary syndrome event. Patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive oral milvexian (25 mg twice daily) or matched placebo. The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke as evaluated in a time-to-event analysis. The principal safety outcome was Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 3c or 5 bleeding (intracranial or intraocular bleeding that compromises vision or fatal bleeding).

RESULTS: After a planned interim analysis that was based on 556 adjudicated efficacy end points, the trial was terminated for futility. A total of 14,194 patients had been enrolled, with 7094 assigned to receive milvexian and 7100 to receive placebo. After a median follow-up of 12.2 months, a primary efficacy outcome event had occurred in 384 patients (5.4%) in the milvexian group and in 365 patients (5.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.05; 95% confidence interval, 0.91 to 1.21; P = 0.50). BARC type 3c or 5 bleeding occurred in 23 patients (0.3%) in the milvexian group and in 22 patients (0.3%) in the placebo group (P = 0.88).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome event, milvexian did not decrease the risk of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke but did not increase the risk of intracranial or fatal bleeding, as compared with placebo. (Funded by Janssen Research and Development and Bristol Myers Squibb; LIBREXIA ACS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05754957.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608717.summary: Among patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome event, milvexian did not decrease the risk of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke but did not increase the risk of intracranial or fatal bleeding, as compared with placebo.
10.1056/nejmoa2608717.title: Milvexian with Antiplatelet Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndrome Event

10.1056/nejmoa2608903.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Many patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome in whom myocardial infarction has been ruled out in the emergency department remain at risk for cardiovascular events. Whether further investigation reduces this risk is unknown.

METHODS: In a multicenter, randomized, controlled trial, patients who presented to an emergency department in 14 hospitals across the United Kingdom were enrolled if myocardial infarction had been ruled out and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin testing indicated an intermediate risk of a cardiovascular event (maximum high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I or T concentration, >5 ng per liter). Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either outpatient computed tomographic (CT) coronary angiography-guided care or standard care. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction or death from a cardiac cause.

RESULTS: From September 18, 2019, to May 11, 2023, a total of 3170 participants (median age, 61 years; female sex, 30.2%) were assigned to undergo CT coronary angiography (1587 participants) or receive standard care (1583 participants). At 90 days after randomization, CT coronary angiography had been performed in 1462 participants (92.1%) in the CT coronary angiography group and in 35 participants (2.2%) in the standard-care group. Overall, 7 participants (0.4%) had a CT coronary angiography-related adverse event. After a median of 3.0 years, at which point the number of primary-outcome events in the standard-care group exceeded the prespecified minimum of 97, a primary-outcome event had occurred in 112 participants (7.1%) in the CT coronary angiography group and in 116 (7.3%) in the standard-care group (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval, 0.73 to 1.23; P = 0.71).

CONCLUSIONS: In patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome in whom myocardial infarction had been ruled out, routine CT coronary angiography-guided management did not result in a lower incidence of subsequent myocardial infarction or death from a cardiac cause than standard care. (Funded by the British Heart Foundation; TARGET-CTCA ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03952351.).
10.1056/nejmoa2608903.summary: In patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome in whom myocardial infarction had been ruled out, routine CT coronary angiography-guided management did not result in a lower incidence of subsequent myocardial infarction or death from a cardiac cause than standard care.
10.1056/nejmoa2608903.title: Targeted Use of Computed Tomographic Coronary Angiography in Acute Chest Pain

10.1056/nejmoa2609056.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary hypertension that is caused by left heart disease and is associated with heart failure may be driven by sympathetic overactivation leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular dysfunction, and poor outcomes. Pulmonary-artery denervation may reduce sympathetic activity, although its clinical effects on left heart disease-associated pulmonary hypertension are unknown.

METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, randomized trial in China involving patients with pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease and heart failure. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive pulmonary-artery denervation plus guideline-directed medical therapy or to receive medical therapy alone. The primary outcome was clinical worsening - a composite of death, heart or lung transplantation, hospitalization for heart failure, outpatient worsening of heart failure, or a decline in the 6-minute walk distance - through the latest follow-up.

RESULTS: A total of 264 patients underwent randomization: 134 to receive pulmonary-artery denervation plus medical therapy and 130 to receive medical therapy alone. During a median follow-up of 338 days, the Kaplan-Meier estimated 2-year incidence of clinical worsening was 25.7% in the pulmonary-artery denervation group and 51.5% in the medical-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.49; 95% confidence interval, 0.30 to 0.82; P = 0.006). Access-site hematomas occurred in two patients in the pulmonary-artery denervation group and in one patient in the medical-therapy group; there were no other procedural complications. Adverse events during follow-up occurred with similar frequency in the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease and heart failure receiving guideline-directed medical therapy, pulmonary-artery denervation resulted in fewer events of clinical worsening than medical therapy. (Funded by Pulnovo Medical and others; PADN-HF-PH ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05824923.).
10.1056/nejmoa2609056.summary: Among patients with pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease and heart failure receiving guideline-directed medical therapy, pulmonary-artery denervation resulted in fewer events of clinical worsening than medical therapy.
10.1056/nejmoa2609056.title: Pulmonary Denervation for Heart Failure–Related Pulmonary Hypertension

10.1056/nejmoa2609057.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether prasugrel or ticagrelor should be the preferred P2Y12 inhibitor for patients with an acute coronary syndrome is uncertain.

METHODS: We conducted a registry-based, open-label, stepped-wedge, cluster-randomized trial in Sweden involving adults who had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention for an acute coronary syndrome. Seven regions, grouped into three clusters, switched from ticagrelor to prasugrel as the default P2Y12 inhibitor in a randomized sequence across four 9-month periods between 2021 and 2024. The primary end point was a composite of death from any cause, fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, or fatal or nonfatal stroke through 1 year, as ascertained from national registries. In the intention-to-treat analysis, a mixed model adjusted for cluster and calendar time was used to obtain a policy-level estimate.

RESULTS: A total of 17,095 patients were enrolled; 9444 received care under the default ticagrelor policy, and 7651 received care under the default prasugrel policy. The mean (±SD) age of the patients was 69.8±11.5 years, and 36.8% were at least 75 years old; 27.8% of the patients were female. A total of 39.4% presented with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), 43.7% with non-STEMI, and 16.8% with unstable angina. At 1 year, a primary end-point event had occurred in 11.8% of the patients in the ticagrelor-policy group and in 11.1% of those in the prasugrel-policy group (adjusted odds ratio [prasugrel vs. ticagrelor], 0.90; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.77 to 1.06), and major bleeding had occurred in 4.4% and 4.2%, respectively (adjusted odds ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.99).

CONCLUSIONS: In an unselected population of patients with an acute coronary syndrome who had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention, the risk of ischemic events was not lower with a default prasugrel policy than with a default ticagrelor policy. (Funded by Region Västra Götaland; SWITCH-SWEDEHEART ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05183178.).
10.1056/nejmoa2609057.summary: In an unselected population of patients with an acute coronary syndrome who had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention, the risk of ischemic events was not lower with a default prasugrel policy than with a default ticagrelor policy.
10.1056/nejmoa2609057.title: Prasugrel versus Ticagrelor in Acute Coronary Syndromes

10.1056/nejmoa2609059.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atherosclerosis may begin in early adulthood and remain clinically silent for decades before cardiovascular disease manifests. Although silent atherosclerosis is associated with cardiovascular events and death independent of traditional cardiovascular disease risk factors, its age- and sex-specific prevalence, vascular territory distribution, and plaque volume across adult life remain incompletely defined.

METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study in Denmark and Spain. Adults 18 to 70 years of age without known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were enrolled in five prespecified age strata that included balanced numbers of women and men. Silent atherosclerosis was assessed at baseline with three-dimensional vascular ultrasonography of the carotid and femoral arteries and with coronary computed tomographic angiography.

RESULTS: A total of 16,808 adults were enrolled in the study. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 45±12 years, and 51.4% were women. Silent atherosclerosis was present in 57.1% of the participants (95% confidence interval, 56.3 to 58.0). In the youngest age stratum (18 to 29 years), atherosclerosis was present in 8.7% of the men and 6.7% of the women; prevalence increased with age, with a later, steeper midlife rise among women. Among participants in the younger age strata, atherosclerosis was most often peripheral and confined to a single vascular territory; with increasing age, plaque volume increased exponentially and the prevalence of multiarterial involvement became more frequent. Isolated coronary-artery atherosclerosis was uncommon in every age stratum (≤9.3% of men and ≤5.0% of women).

CONCLUSIONS: This study of silent atherosclerosis showed that the disease was detectable in early adulthood, with age- and sex-associated increases in prevalence across arterial territories and marked increases in plaque volume. (Funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation; REACT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06692127.).
10.1056/nejmoa2609059.summary: This study of silent atherosclerosis showed that the disease was detectable in early adulthood, with age- and sex-associated increases in prevalence across arterial territories and marked increases in plaque volume.
10.1056/nejmoa2609059.title: Prevalence of Silent Atherosclerosis across Adult Life

10.1056/nejmoa2609127.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sibeprenlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, selectively inhibits the cytokine A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), a key driver of IgA nephropathy. Preliminary trial results with regard to the primary end point of the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at 9 months after treatment as compared with baseline have been reported, but secondary end points, including outcomes regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), have not.

METHODS: We randomly assigned adults with IgA nephropathy to receive subcutaneous sibeprenlimab (at a dose of 400 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks. The key secondary end point was the annualized slope of the eGFR over 24 months. Other secondary end points included the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months, a composite kidney end point of kidney-function decline or kidney failure, and pharmacodynamic and safety end points.

RESULTS: A total of 510 patients underwent randomization - 259 to receive sibeprenlimab and 251 to receive placebo. The annualized eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area per year (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year (95% CI, -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference, 4.5 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001). The least-squares mean treatment difference for the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months was 9.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, 7.1 to 11.4; P<0.001). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the sibeprenlimab group and in 28 patients (11.2%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -10.8 percentage points; hazard ratio, 0.029; 95% CI, 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 235 patients (90.7%) in the sibeprenlimab group and 226 patients (90.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 21 patients (8.1%) and 32 patients (12.7%), respectively; and serious infections in 5 patients (1.9%) and 10 patients (4.0%). No deaths were reported.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline. (Funded by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization; VISIONARY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05248646.).
10.1056/nejmoa2609127.summary: Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline.
10.1056/nejmoa2609127.title: Sibeprenlimab in IgA Nephropathy — Final Phase 3 Trial Analysis

10.1056/nejmoa2609149.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether endovascular therapy benefits patients with mild acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion involving the anterior circulation is uncertain.

METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial in China involving patients with acute ischemic stroke of mild clinical severity (defined by a score of <6 on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) that had resulted from large-vessel occlusion involving the anterior circulation. Patients also had neuroimaging features of a small infarct core and a large perfusion-mismatch volume, representing substantial at-risk tissue, within 24 hours after symptom onset or after they were last known to be well. The patients were randomly assigned to undergo endovascular therapy and receive medical management or to receive medical management alone. The primary outcome was an excellent functional outcome (defined by a modified Rankin scale score of 0 [no symptoms] or 1 [no clinically significant disability]) at 90 days.

RESULTS: A total of 304 patients underwent randomization, of whom 300 were included in the modified intention-to-treat population: 144 in the endovascular-therapy group and 156 in the medical-management group. At 90 days, a modified Rankin scale score of 0 or 1 was reported in 69.4% of the patients in the endovascular-therapy group and in 50.0% of those in the medical-management group (odds ratio, 2.32; 95% confidence interval, 1.41 to 3.81; P<0.001). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 48 hours occurred in 3 patients in each group. Serious procedure-related complications occurred in 19 patients (13.2%) in the endovascular-therapy group. Among all the participants, one death occurred (in the endovascular-therapy group).

CONCLUSIONS: In this trial from China involving patients with mild acute ischemic stroke caused by large-vessel occlusion and substantial at-risk tissue on perfusion imaging, endovascular therapy performed within 24 hours after symptom onset plus medical management resulted in better 90-day functional outcomes than medical management alone, without an increase in the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage but with a high incidence of serious procedural complications. (Funded by Fujian Medical University Union Hospital and others; MILD-MT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06179017.).

10.1056/nejmoa2609149.title: Trial of Endovascular Therapy for Mild Stroke with Large-Vessel Occlusion

10.1056/nejmoa2609362.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endovascular thrombectomy is an established treatment for acute ischemic stroke. Whether the benefit extends to patients with salvageable brain tissue in the infarct who present more than 24 hours after symptom onset or the time when they were last known to be well is uncertain.

METHODS: We conducted an open-label, randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment at comprehensive stroke centers in China. Patients with acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and imaging-identified salvageable brain tissue at 24 to 72 hours were assigned to receive endovascular therapy plus standard medical care (intervention group) or standard medical care alone (control group). The primary outcome was functional status, defined by the score on the modified Rankin scale (range, 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater disability and a score of 6 indicating death) at 90 days, with results assessed as the distribution of scores in each group. Secondary outcomes included disability, neurologic impairment, and safety.

RESULTS: A total of 336 patients were included in the intention-to-treat population, with 168 assigned to each group. The median time from symptom onset or from the point when the patient was last known to be well to randomization was 38.5 hours. Endovascular therapy resulted in a more favorable distribution of modified Rankin scale scores at 90 days than standard medical care alone (common odds ratio for a better functional outcome, 1.74; 95% confidence interval, 1.19 to 2.55). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 4.8% of the patients in the intervention group and in no patients in the control group, and the 90-day case fatality rate was 6.0% and 1.8%, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who presented 24 to 72 hours after an acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and had imaging-identified salvageable tissue, endovascular therapy resulted in better functional outcomes than standard care but led to a higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage and death. (Funded by the National Health Commission Capacity Building and Continuing Education Center and others; LATE-MT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05326932.).

10.1056/nejmoa2609362.title: Mechanical Thrombectomy 24 to 72 Hours after Large-Vessel Ischemic Stroke

10.1056/nejmoa2609482.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer have poor outcomes, with a median overall survival of approximately 12 to 13 months. Tarlatamab (a bispecific T-cell engager targeting delta-like ligand 3 [DLL3] and CD3) was previously shown to improve survival as second-line therapy. Whether adding tarlatamab to durvalumab (an anti-programmed death ligand 1 agent) after initial chemoimmunotherapy could significantly improve survival in the context of maintenance therapy after first remission has been unclear.

METHODS: In this phase 3, international, open-label, randomized trial, we compared tarlatamab-durvalumab with durvalumab as first-line maintenance therapy in patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer without progression after initial chemoimmunotherapy. Overall survival and progression-free survival were assessed from randomization at the start of maintenance therapy as the primary and key secondary end points, respectively. Results of the prespecified interim analysis (data-cutoff date, July 7, 2026) are reported here.

RESULTS: A total of 563 patients were randomly assigned to receive tarlatamab-durvalumab (282 patients) or durvalumab (281 patients). At a median follow-up of 15.9 months in the tarlatamab-durvalumab group and 16.1 months in the durvalumab group, the estimated median overall survival was 21.1 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 20.8 to could not be estimated) with tarlatamab-durvalumab and 12.7 months (95% CI, 11.2 to 14.8) with durvalumab (hazard ratio for death, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.32 to 0.54; P<0.001). The median progression-free survival was 7.4 months (95% CI, 5.6 to 9.1) with tarlatamab-durvalumab and 1.9 months (95% CI, 1.9 to 2.0) with durvalumab (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.28 to 0.42; P<0.001). Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 46.8% of the patients who received tarlatamab-durvalumab and in 40.6% of those who received durvalumab alone. Cytokine release syndrome, mainly of grade 1 or 2, was seen in nearly half the patients receiving tarlatamab-durvalumab.

CONCLUSIONS: Tarlatamab-durvalumab maintenance therapy resulted in significantly longer overall survival and progression-free survival than durvalumab alone among patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. (Funded by Amgen and AstraZeneca; DeLLphi-305 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06211036.).
10.1056/nejmoa2609482.summary: Tarlatamab-durvalumab maintenance therapy resulted in significantly longer overall survival and progression-free survival than durvalumab alone among patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer.
10.1056/nejmoa2609482.title: Tarlatamab–Durvalumab Maintenance for Extensive-Stage Small-Cell Lung Cancer

10.1056/nejmoa2610103.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here.

METHODS: We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed.

RESULTS: Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m2; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died.

CONCLUSIONS: Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).
10.1056/nejmoa2610103.summary: Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo.
10.1056/nejmoa2610103.title: Atacicept in IgA Nephropathy — Phase 3 Trial Final Efficacy Analysis

10.1056/nejmoa2610229.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tambotatug pelitecan (known as Tam-Peli, a new antibody-drug conjugate that targets the immune-checkpoint molecule B7-H3) showed promising clinical efficacy in patients with relapsed extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in early-phase trials.

METHODS: In this phase 3, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial, we assigned eligible patients with small-cell lung cancer that had progressed after first-line platinum-based therapy in a 1:1 ratio to receive tambotatug pelitecan or topotecan. The primary end point was overall survival. The key secondary end points were progression-free survival and objective response as assessed by investigators. Here, we report the results from the prespecified interim analysis.

RESULTS: A total of 451 patients underwent randomization: 225 were assigned to receive tambotatug pelitecan and 226 to receive topotecan. Overall survival was significantly longer with tambotatug pelitecan than with topotecan - a median of 13.3 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.1 to could not be estimated), as compared with 9.4 months (95% CI, 7.7 to 10.5); the stratified hazard ratio for death was 0.46 (95% CI, 0.35 to 0.62; P<0.001). Treatment with tambotatug pelitecan also resulted in significantly longer progression-free survival than treatment with topotecan (median, 7.4 months [95% CI, 6.1 to 7.6] vs. 2.8 months [95% CI, 1.8 to 3.0]; stratified hazard ratio, 0.29 [95% CI, 0.23 to 0.37]; P<0.001). A confirmed objective response occurred in 59.1% of the patients in the tambotatug pelitecan group, as compared with 9.7% of those in the topotecan group (P<0.001). The overall incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was lower with tambotatug pelitecan than with topotecan (55.4% vs. 77.9%).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with relapsed small-cell lung cancer after platinum-based therapy, treatment with tambotatug pelitecan resulted in longer overall survival, longer progression-free survival, and a higher percentage of patients with an objective response than treatment with topotecan, with a lower incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher. (Funded by the Innovative Drug Research and Development National Science and Technology Major Project and MediLink Therapeutics; TAISHAN-302 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06612151.).

10.1056/nejmoa2610229.title: Tambotatug Pelitecan in Small-Cell Lung Cancer after Platinum-Based Therapy

10.1056/nejmoa2610345.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The combination of docetaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab (THP) is an established first-line treatment for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive advanced breast cancer. The efficacy and safety of anbenitamab, a HER2-targeted bispecific antibody, plus albumin-bound docetaxel (HB1801) in this context are unknown.

METHODS: In this phase 3, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in China, we randomly assigned patients with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer in a 1:1 ratio to receive either anbenitamab plus HB1801 or THP. The primary end point was progression-free survival, as assessed by blinded independent central review. Objective response was a secondary end point.

RESULTS: A total of 885 patients were enrolled (445 were assigned to receive anbenitamab plus HB1801 and 440 to receive THP). At this prespecified interim analysis (with 401 events [disease progression or death] and a median follow-up of 21.0 months), the estimated 24-month progression-free survival was significantly higher with anbenitamab plus HB1801 than with THP (58.5% vs. 34.4%; hazard ratio for progression or death, 0.46; 95% confidence interval, 0.37 to 0.56; P<0.001). The percentage of patients with an objective response was 87.6% in the anbenitamab group and 73.4% in the THP group. Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 204 of 444 patients (45.9%) in the anbenitamab group and in 151 of 439 patients (34.4%) in the THP group. Neutropenia was the most common adverse event of grade 3 or higher in both groups (13.1% in the anbenitamab group and 8.4% in the THP group). Adverse events leading to death occurred in 2 patients in each group.

CONCLUSIONS: Anbenitamab plus HB1801 led to significantly higher progression-free survival than THP among patients with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer. (Funded by Shanghai JMT-Bio Technology and others; HEALER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05838066.).
10.1056/nejmoa2610345.summary: Anbenitamab plus HB1801 led to significantly higher progression-free survival than THP among patients with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer.
10.1056/nejmoa2610345.title: Anbenitamab plus HB1801 for HER2-Positive Advanced Breast Cancer

10.1056/nejmoa2611280.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy with a platinum-based agent and pemetrexed is a widely used standard first-line treatment option for patients with programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1)-negative advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without targetable genomic alterations, but outcomes remain suboptimal.

METHODS: In this phase 3, open-label, randomized trial, we evaluated sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab in patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC without targetable genomic alterations and a PD-L1 tumor proportion score of less than 1%. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab or chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab. The primary end point was progression-free survival as assessed by blinded independent central review. Overall survival was a secondary end point. This report presents the results of the prespecified interim analysis.

RESULTS: A total of 455 patients were randomly assigned to receive sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab (229 patients) or chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (226 patients). After a median follow-up of 9.7 months, the median progression-free survival was significantly longer with sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab than with chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (15.0 months vs. 5.7 months; hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.49; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.36 to 0.65; P<0.001). An objective response occurred in 50.2% and 47.3% of the patients, respectively, and the median duration of response was 13.6 months and 6.8 months. Overall survival data were immature; the hazard ratio for death was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.88). Adverse events of grade 3 or higher that occurred after the start of treatment were reported in 47.6% of the patients assigned to receive sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab and in 60.6% of those assigned to receive chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab. Stomatitis was common with sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab, but the events were predominantly grade 1 or 2.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with PD-L1-negative advanced nonsquamous NSCLC without targetable genomic alterations, first-line treatment with sacituzumab tirumotecan plus pembrolizumab led to significantly longer progression-free survival than chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab. (Funded by Sichuan Kelun-Biotech Biopharmaceutical; OptiTROP-Lung06 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06711900.).

10.1056/nejmoa2611335.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Savolitinib is an oral, potent, highly selective MET-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI). Combination therapy with savolitinib and osimertinib, an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-TKI, has shown activity in patients with EGFR-mutated, advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with MET overexpression, MET amplification, or both, after progression during EGFR-TKI therapy.

METHODS: In this international, phase 3, open-label trial, we randomly assigned, in a 1:1 ratio, patients with EGFR-mutated, locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with MET overexpression (staining intensity of 3+ for MET in ≥90% of tumor cells on immunohistochemical analysis), MET amplification (≥10 gene copies on fluorescence in situ hybridization), or both whose disease had progressed during osimertinib therapy to receive osimertinib (at a dose of 80 mg once daily) plus savolitinib (300 mg twice daily) or intravenous platinum-pemetrexed. The primary end point was progression-free survival, as assessed by blinded independent central review. Secondary end points included overall survival and safety.

RESULTS: Of the 1746 patients screened, 338 were randomly assigned to receive osimertinib-savolitinib (171 patients) or platinum-pemetrexed (167 patients). Osimertinib-savolitinib led to significantly longer progression-free survival than platinum-pemetrexed (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42 to 0.72; P<0.001), as well as significantly longer overall survival (hazard ratio for death, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.50 to 0.91; P = 0.01; final analysis). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of 12-month progression-free survival was 36% in the osimertinib-savolitinib group and 10% in the platinum-pemetrexed group, and the estimate of 12-month overall survival was 70% and 53%, respectively. The most frequently reported adverse events that occurred during treatment in the osimertinib-savolitinib group were peripheral edema (in 49% of the patients), anemia (in 26%), and diarrhea (in 26%). Grade 3 or higher adverse events during treatment were reported in 64% of the patients in the osimertinib-savolitinib group and in 63% of those in the platinum-pemetrexed group.

CONCLUSIONS: Osimertinib-savolitinib led to significantly longer progression-free and overall survival than platinum-pemetrexed among patients with EGFR-mutated, locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with MET overexpression, MET amplification, or both that had progressed during osimertinib therapy (Funded by AstraZeneca; SAFFRON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05261399.).

10.1056/nejmoa2611477.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

METHODS: In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results.

RESULTS: A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.

CONCLUSIONS: In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag708.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations.

RESULTS: We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79 648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing.

AVAILABILITY: CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag722.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses.

RESULTS: We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS, with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag730.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data.

RESULTS: Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations.

AVAILABILITY: Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681. Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872.

MOTIVATION: Existing methods for batch effect removal often suffer from an ill-defined problem formulation and rely on unverified assumptions, limiting their robustness and generalizability. This study proposes a principled approach to systematically address these limitations.

RESULTS: We present two novel methodologies for removing systematic batch effects: an unsupervised approach based on independent component analysis and a supervised approach using a domain adaptation technique. Both methods are grounded in rigorous mathematical principles. Our approaches outperforms existing methods across multiple datasets.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The implementation of our methods, including all code, datasets, experimental workflows, and supplementary material, is available in Python and has been made publicly accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/shaham-lab/revisiting-batch-effect-removal, Supplementary Material: https://github.com/shaham-lab/revisiting-batch-effect-removal/blob/main/proofs/suplementery_matirial.pdf.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag750.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounder, antibiotic use.

RESULTS: To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag750.summary: Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag750.title: Inverse probability weighting-based mediation analysis for microbiome data

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag751.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism for their risk is through cellular context-dependent epigenetics such as methylation. Previous methodologies have focused on integrating GWAS with single cell transcriptomics, which allowed identification of within-cell-type heterogeneity in disease risk association. We extended this framework to provide a method called met-scDRS that integrates GWAS with single cell epigenomics and investigates how psychiatric disease risk can manifest through methylomics at single cell resolution.

RESULTS: We propose an approach that integrates single cell methylomes with disease associated genes identified from GWAS at single-cell resolution. We found our method to be well calibrated and powered in different scenarios. We then analysed a publicly available single cell methylome dataset of the human brain for 75 different traits and generated disease relevance scores for each cell for each trait. We find high brain specificity with major cell type enrichments congruent with known findings. We identify within-cell-type heterogeneity for psychiatric disease risk along the brain spatial axis as well as subpopulations that are differentially associated with diseases. Finally, we showed that genes with high correlation between methylation levels and disease relevance scores to be highly enriched in specific functional pathways such as synaptic formation and transmission.

AVAILABILITY: met-scDRS is freely available in GitHub as a python package under MIT license: https://github.com/bogdanlab/met-scDRS. Source code is also available from Zenodo with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21841506. All dataset used in this work are publicly available.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag753.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Sequencing-based epigenomic profiling methods are powerful but suffer from technical variability that complicates cross-sample comparisons and can obscure true biological signals. While existing normalization methods using spike-in controls or computational approaches have been proposed, they often rely on assumptions that may not hold across diverse experimental conditions or require additional data types.

RESULTS: We present Ryder, a flexible and robust Python package for the normalization of epigenomic signal tracks. Ryder leverages stable internal reference regions, such as invariant CTCF binding sites, to correct for technical artifacts genome-wide. Our results show that it effectively adjusts both background noise and signal intensity, ensuring accurate signal alignment across samples while preserving genuine biological differences. We demonstrate that Ryder performs robustly across diverse assays including DNase-seq, CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, MNase-seq, and ChIP-seq, with or without spike-in controls. By reducing technical noise, Ryder improves the detection of genuine biological changes, such as quantitative reduction of chromatin accessibility at key enhancer elements by depletion of BRG1, a key subunit of the chromatin remodeling BAF complexes.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The Ryder source code, documentation and test data are freely available at: https://github.com/YaqiangCao/ryder. The software version used in this study is archived at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21267457.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag753.summary: We present Ryder, a flexible and robust Python package for the normalization of epigenomic signal tracks.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag753.title: Ryder: epigenome normalization using a two-tier model and internal reference regions

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag754.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Determining the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins is a cornerstone of structural biology, providing essential insights into their underlying biological mechanisms and functional roles. Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis allows researchers to investigate biomolecules at near-atomic resolutions, unraveling the structure of biomolecular complexes. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D volumes from extremely noisy projections, particularly under the interference of structural heterogeneity, remains a challenging task. Traditional Fourier-domain methods often suffer from frequency-dependent signal attenuation and uneven information distribution. While recent deep-learning-based frameworks attempt to predict high-frequency components directly in frequency space, they are highly susceptible to noise and often introduce artifacts. State-of-the-art (SOTA) real-space method circumvents Fourier-domain defects, yet remains constrained by the inherent spectral bias of multi-layer perceptrons, as fixed positional encoding fails to sufficiently capture intricate high-frequency details.

RESULTS: We propose cryoTriplane, a real-space 3D homogeneous reconstruction network that utilizes a hybrid spatial representation to adaptively capture fine structural details. By combining fixed positional encoding for noise-robust structural initialization with structure-aware positional encoding for high-frequency refinement, our method achieves 3D reconstructions that are simultaneously globally consistent and locally fine-grained. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations across five simulated and four real-world datasets demonstrate that cryoTriplane significantly outperforms existing methods in resolving fine structural features. Furthermore, validation through downstream atomic modeling underscores cryoTriplane's ability to recover high-quality density maps. Specifically, our method achieves sequence coverage improvements of 4.6% and 5.5% on the EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10492 datasets over the SOTA approach, respectively.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Our code is available at https://github.com/chengyr1999/CryoTriplane. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag755.abstract:
MOTIVATION: De novo peptide sequencing from tandem mass spectra is essential for characterizing unknown proteins, identifying novel post-translational modifications, and analysing samples without reference databases. While recent deep learning models have improved the predicted peptide accuracy, they typically select the predicted peptide sequence based solely on sequence-level decoding scores. Very often, high scores are assigned to peptides without the direct support from the observed mass spectrum.

RESULTS: We present "ScopeNovo", a de novo peptide sequencing method that improves predicted peptide accuracy by using spectrum-spectrum similarity between the input spectrum and the "representative" spectrum corresponding to the predicted peptide sequence. ScopeNovo generates multiple candidate peptides using an existing peptide de novo sequencing learning model and reranks candidates based on spectrum-spectrum similarity. To test our method, we use π-PrimeNovo as the base learning model. Experimental results on the standard nine-species benchmark datasets V1 and V2 show that ScopeNovo can substantially improve the prediction accuracy. We designed two settings, where Setting 1 is for well-annotated species, and Setting 2 is for species that are not well annotated. For Setting 1, ScopeNovo improves the average peptide accuracies of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 6.1% and 4.0% on V1 and V2, respectively. For Setting 2, ScopeNovo can still improve the peptide accuracy of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 3.4% and 1.9% on the V1 and V2 benchmark datasets, respectively. Compared to the best-known method, RankNovo, the peptide accuracies over the nine species on V1 and V2 of our method for Setting 1 are 0.711 and 0.737, where the peptide accuracies for RankNovo are 0.687 and 0.682. Even for Setting 2, the peptide accuracies of our method are comparable to those of RankNovo.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: ScopeNovo is implemented in Python under an MIT license. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/SoSongzhi/ScopeNovo.git. The test data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23181841.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag759.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Automated cytology screening is essential for early cervical cancer prevention, where gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) are typically partitioned into tiles for tile-level feature extraction and subsequent WSI-level diagnosis aggregation. However, existing tile-level methods remain constrained by limited input sizes, which frequently obscures sparse and morphologically subtle abnormal cells. Furthermore, these methods commonly formulate tile-level representation learning as a coarse single-label classification task, thereby failing to capture the complex co-occurrence patterns and morphological heterogeneity of cervical cytological abnormalities.

RESULTS: We propose the Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning Network (FMCerNet), a tile-level feature extractor equipped with a Large-Field Frequency-Enhanced ViT (LFreq-ViT) backbone and a Coarse-to-Fine multi-label classification (C2F) head. The former incorporates a Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform module to efficiently extract frequency-domain features from large-scale tiles, whereas the latter enhances fine-grained tile representation decoding through hierarchical supervision. Experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate that FMCerNet improves the accuracy of positive screening and fine-grained subtype classification while maintaining high inference speed.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code at https://github.com/imAzhou/FMCerNet and archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22886105).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary files are available with the manuscript.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag759.title: FMCerNet: Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning for Fine-Grained Cervical Cytology Screening

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag765.abstract:
MOTIVATION: (Cryo-)FIB/SEM enables 3D ultrastructural analysis of cells and tissues at nanoscale resolution. However, its characteristically low signal-to-noise ratio severely hinders interpretation of the volume data. Noise2Noise (N2N) has emerged as a state-of-the-art denoising paradigm with outstanding performance in 3D electron microscopy-particularly cryo-ET-but its direct application to (cryo-)FIB/SEM remains unfeasible due to the inherent acquisition workflows.

RESULTS: A method to enable N2N denoising in (cryo-)FIB/SEM is introduced. The input volume is split into even and odd slices, followed by the application of motion correction methods to estimate and compensate for the structural differences between the two subvolumes. The resulting motion-corrected subvolumes are then used to train the N2N model, which is ultimately applied to denoise the original volume. Representative (cryo-)FIB/SEM volumes have been used to validate the method and to demonstrate the critical importance of the motion correction stage for volumes with a slice thickness >10 nm.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag767.abstract:
SUMMARY: Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) and its successor ANCOM-BC2 are critical algorithms for differential abundance analysis. Designed for handling compositional data, they feature the ability to estimate the unknown sampling fractions and correct the bias induced by their differences. While the original R package implementing the two methods is robust for standard dataset sizes, the increasing magnitude of modern multiomics studies presents computational challenges, often resulting in a runtime bottleneck for high-dimensional data. Here, we present native Python implementations of both ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 in the scikit-bio package, significantly accelerating the workflow and enabling their application to large-scale datasets. By leveraging vectorization with NumPy and numerical optimization in SciPy, we enhanced the efficiency of both methods without compromising their statistical accuracy. The benchmarking results revealed a dramatic increase in performance in both simulated and real datasets. We demonstrated that our Python implementations generated test results matching the original R code, while achieving 380- and 147-fold faster runtimes and 97.4% and 96.2% lower memory consumption on the largest tested dataset, respectively. The Python implementations allow for the analysis of datasets that are significantly larger than previously possible, and enable applications to alternative omics data types and complex statistical models that vary greatly by the number of samples, features, and covariates.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: https://github.com/scikit-bio/scikit-bio.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag768.abstract:
MOTIVATION: We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph.

RESULTS: Semantic representations of term names, combined with UMAP visualization and k-means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal-Wallis H=5244, p<10-300; η2=0.217). Term-name length increased with depth (Pearson r=0.34, Spearman ρ=0.37; slope ≈3.2 letters per level), and this positive scaling held under shortest-, longest-, and average-path depth definitions. Vocabulary entropy followed a bell-shaped diversification-specialization curve with an intermediate-depth peak (maximal at depth 4) that lies outside a Monte Carlo null envelope across most depths, and null-model tests supported a genuine linguistic-hierarchical association.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag769.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Accurate enzyme function annotation is critical for interpreting rapidly expanding sequence data, yet experimental methods are costly and low-throughput, while computational approaches face two key limitations. Most existing methods are discriminative models confined to known EC labels, making it difficult to generalize to emerging enzymatic activities under cold-start conditions. Moreover, they typically treat enzymes as isolated molecular entities and overlook microenvironment factors such as optimal pH and temperature, which provide important contextual clues for functional annotation.

RESULTS: This study proposes MPA-EC, a generative framework that integrates microenvironment as pragmatic context into enzyme function reasoning. By fine-tuning the large language model on a newly constructed Enzyme Microenvironment Database, the model learns to infer microenvironment from sequence and then reason function within that context, generating EC labels with explicit reasoning chains. MEMP imputes missing pH and temperature values to complete the Enzyme Microenvironment Database. On public benchmark dataset, MPA-EC achieves an absolute F1 improvement of 0.1068 over the state-of-the-art GraphEC model. Under cold-start conditions, the model generates reference-worthy function labels, demonstrating its practical utility for emerging enzymatic activities.

AVAILABILITY: The source code and data of MPA-EC can be accessed at https://bliulab.net/MPA-EC, https://zenodo.org/records/22152329 and https://github.com/bliulab/MPA-EC.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag769.summary: Under cold-start conditions, the model generates reference-worthy function labels, demonstrating its practical utility for emerging enzymatic activities.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag769.title: Microenvironment Awareness Pragmatic Analysis for Generative Enzyme Function Reasoning

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag771.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Quantifying predictive uncertainty is essential for computational drug discovery to reduce experimental costs and false positives. However, most drug-target affinity (DTA) models focus on improving prediction accuracy without reliable uncertainty estimates.

RESULTS: We propose RCP-DTA, a representation-aware conformal prediction framework that constructs adaptive prediction intervals based on feature similarity. By constructing local calibration sets, our approach generates sample-specific prediction intervals that achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal confidence level. To enhance representation quality, RCP-DTA employs a cross-modal architecture that integrates pre-trained sequence representations and structural information. Binding site context is incorporated via virtual pocket feedback to enhance residue representations, followed by gated fusion for adaptive integration of sequence and structural modalities. Evaluations across multiple DTA benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCP-DTA achieves competitive affinity prediction performance while providing reliable uncertainty quantification.

AVAILABILITY: Code and data are available at: https://github.com/Lee515628/RCP-DTA.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag771.title: Representation-aware conformal prediction for reliable uncertainty quantification in drug-target affinity

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag772.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Single-cell time-series atlases provide discrete cross-sectional snapshots of continuous developmental processes, making missing-snapshot prediction essential for reconstructing trajectories and dynamic programs. However, destructive scRNA-seq profiling prevents tracking the same cells across time, yielding unpaired population snapshots and making missing-snapshot prediction challenging. Existing methods typically rely on explicit dynamical propagation or transport-based coupling between snapshots, which may ignore the statistical constraints of the overall population distribution and be sensitive to sampling noise and cell-to-cell variability.

RESULTS: We introduce scChronos, a hierarchical temporal context learning framework that formulates missing-snapshot prediction as target-conditioned population distribution prediction rather than individual-cell propagation. Unlike cell-centric propagation approaches, scChronos explicitly captures dual-level dynamics: (i) Within each observed snapshot, scChronos compresses cell populations into cluster-representative cell representations with a transcriptomic encoder, preserving population information while reducing noise; (ii) Across reference snapshots, the dual-branch temporal context integration module fuses information from all available and nearby time points into a temporal representation, which is then decoded with learnable cell-generation seeds to predict the target distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that scChronos improves both interpolation-style recovery and extrapolation-style forecasting compared with state-of-the-art methods. Beyond reducing distributional discrepancy, scChronos better preserves developmental topology and maintains cell-type-specific marker and pathway programs.

AVAILABILITY: The code and data are available at https://github.com/yjs193/scChronos and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20933283.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag772.summary: Beyond reducing distributional discrepancy, scChronos better preserves developmental topology and maintains cell-type-specific marker and pathway programs.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag772.title: scChronos: Hierarchical Temporal Context Learning for Missing Snapshot Prediction in Single-Cell Time Series

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag774.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Recent advances in biological foundation models have enabled new opportunities for data-driven molecular engineering. However, designing programmable RNA devices remains challenging because of the vast, nonlinear sequence-structure-function landscape. Here, we present Ernie-Switcher, a deep learning framework built upon the RNA foundation model (RNAErnie), comprising three coupled components: (i) integration of RNAErnie-derived sequence-phenotype representations for realistic design generation and filtering; (ii) characterization of RNA landscape navigability as a theoretical basis for sequence optimization; and (iii) incorporation of biophysical constraints to maintain optimization trajectories within biologically plausible bounds.

RESULTS: We validated Ernie-Switcher using RNA toehold switches. Theoretically, the observed lower bound on threshold navigability (86.4%) of the RNA landscape supports the theoretical feasibility of RNA switch sequence optimization. Experimentally, the optimized toehold switches achieved ON/OFF expression ratios of up to 35-fold in Escherichia coli. Collectively, RNAErnie-guided sequence optimization provides a scalable strategy for engineering high-performance RNA devices. To facilitate broad adoption, we deployed Ernie-Switcher as a freely accessible web platform.

AVAILABILITY: The Python code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zhutiblah/Ernie-Switcher and are archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21859277. The RNA toehold switch design platform is available at https://ernie-switcher.bioinformatics-syn.org/.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag774.title: Ernie-Switcher: RNA foundation model-guided design of programmable RNA devices in a navigable landscape

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag775.abstract: The R package MSCquartets offers a suite of methods for testing and inferring species relationships from gene trees under coalescent models. MSCquartets 3.3 significantly extends the functionality of version 1.0 by implementing the TINNiK and ECToBlob algorithms for inference of the tree of blobs under the network multispecies coalescent model (NMSC). Additionally, it implements the NANUQ+ algorithm, a fast method for inference of level-1 networks. Computational speed of all functionalities is greatly improved through use of C ++ routines, and a Shiny App is introduced for easier exploration of basic analyses. Availability and implementation: MSCquartets 3.3 is available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network, at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=MSCquartets. The MSCquartets 3.3 Shiny App is available at https://mscquartets.shinyapps.io/MSCq-app/.
