10.1093/bioinformatics/btag776.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations.

RESULTS: We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag776.summary: We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag776.title: PanRes: A database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag777.abstract:
MOTIVATION: The combinatorial chemistry process called systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) enables the selection of aptamers against different targets. The integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) into SELEX workflows represents a powerful strategy to enhance the identification and prioritization of target-binding aptamers. In this study, we present an optimized computational approach for the NGS-based analysis of enriched aptamer pools generated through SELEX. It encompasses sequencing library preparation, sequence data preprocessing, clustering, multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, and secondary structure prediction.

RESULTS: To identify target-specific aptamers, two comparative analysis strategies were implemented. In the first strategy, sequences detected in the negative selection pool were removed from the positive selection pool to eliminate nonspecific binders, resulting in six distinct sequence clusters. In the second approach, all sequences were retained, and cluster distributions were compared between the positive and negative selection pool, identifying seven clusters in the positive and six in the negative pool. Phylogenetic relationships and structural predictions enabled the selection of promising candidates, which were prioritized based on secondary structure, sequence abundance, and genetic distance from non-specific binders. Binding specificity was assessed through dot blot assays, confirming that the selected aptamers exhibited strong specific binding to the target protein. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the NGS-guided workflow for aptamer discovery and highlight its value in streamlining candidate selection for downstream functional validation.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag777.summary: These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the NGS-guided workflow for aptamer discovery and highlight its value in streamlining candidate selection for downstream functional validation.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag777.title: From SELEX to Sequencing: Uncovering enriched Aptamers with Next-Generation Sequencing and Bioinformatics

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag778.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Protein-ligand binding site prediction (LBS) is important for many areas of structural biology and molecular modeling, where, as in other tasks, protein language models (pLMs) have shown great promise. In their application to LBS, the pLM classifies each amino acid as binding or not, but translating these predictions into three-dimensional binding pockets remains challenging; in particular, residue-centric predictions tend to produce spatially fragmented pockets.

RESULTS: We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing. First, we introduce sc-PDBenhanced, an extended training dataset that augments an existing sc-PDB dataset with additional small-molecule and ion-binding sites, improving coverage of non-obvious and small pockets. Second, we employ an embedding-supported smoothing classifier to refine residue-level predictions. Third, we define the Pocket Fragmentation Index and use it to select a clustering approach that preserves a consistent mapping between predictions and ground-truth pockets. We evaluate Seq2Pocket on two tasks: general binding site prediction using the LIGYSIS benchmark and cryptic binding site prediction using CryptoBench benchmark. Across both benchmarks, Seq2Pocket achieves state-of-the-art DCCtop-N and DCCtop-(N+2) performance. In particular, for general binding site prediction on the LIGYSIS benchmark, it improves distance-center-to-center recall by up to 13%, outperforming existing predictors. This improvement originates from training data quality rather than model architecture, as demonstrated by an ablation study. We believe that these findings contribute to more reliable evaluation practices in ligand binding site prediction, highlight the importance of training data curation, and provide pocket-level prediction tools that are better suited for downstream applications such as drug discovery.

AVAILABILITY: The Seq2Pocket web interface is available at https://seq2pocket.projekty.ms.mff.cuni.cz, running the ESM-2 650M variant. The sc-PDBenhanced is published using Zenodo platform at https://zenodo.org/records/18271517 [Škrhák and Hoksza 2026]. The models are published at HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/skrhakv/seq2pocket.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag778.summary: We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag778.title: Seq2Pocket: augmenting protein language models for spatially consistent binding site prediction

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag779.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Aquatic duckweeds, including Wolffia australiana, are the smallest and fastest growing flowering plants on the planet, with numerous emerging biotechnological applications. Duckweed populations grow through rapid clonal budding, but existing phenotypic characterization and image analysis tools typically operate only at the population level, tracking neither individual plants nor their lineage structure. Deepweed addresses this gap, combining automated individual segmentation, temporal tracking, and clonal lineage reconstruction from time-lapse imaging of duckweed.

RESULTS: Deepweed processes time-lapse duckweed imaging datasets using deep-learning-based instance segmentation and multi-object tracking to assign persistent identities to individual fronds and infer mother-daughter relationships. The workflow outputs lineage graphs, individual-level morphological metrics, and population-level growth summaries, supported by lineage-annotated time-lapse visualizations. Applied to dense Wolffia populations, in both freely growing or controlled microfluidic environments, our framework can track hundreds of Wolffia plants simultaneously, resolves overlapping individuals, and reconstructs multi-generation lineage structure, enabling analyses that are inaccessible with population-level phenotyping methods.

AVAILABILITY: Deepweed is implemented in Python using PyTorch, scikit-image, OpenCV, and btrack. Source code, trained models, example datasets, and documentation are freely available at https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/Deepweed. The Deepweed code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844282 and the datasets are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18843917.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag779.title: Deepweed: Automated Individual Segmentation and Tracking for Duckweed Lineage Analysis

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag781.abstract:
SUMMARY: Deep learning can scale image-based plant phenotyping but typically targets predefined traits, whereas manual phenotypic description is more flexible but difficult to scale. We present Phenotype eXplorer Generative Plant Traits (pxGPT), a Python framework that converts multi-view plant images into structured phenotype records. The workflow combines free-text description, dataset-specific schema generation with human review, and schema-constrained information extraction. We evaluated the extraction stage on three Brassica datasets using 78,973 annotations from ten annotators who had no access to pxGPT predictions. For 38-45 qualitative traits per dataset, pxGPT-human agreement ranged from 0.572 to 0.712, compared with 0.620 to 0.739 agreement among human annotators. All 32,736 required trait fields were present; 93 values were empty, and no qualitative descriptor violations were recorded. For selected morphological structures, pooled false-positive rates were 0.5-8.0%, while sensitivity varied across structure types in one mature-plant dataset (37.5-100%). The curated schemas were applied unchanged with two commercial models and one locally hosted open-weight model, with differences in mean accuracy of 0.03 or less. In the evaluated Brassica datasets, these results support schema-guided extraction of visible plant traits without separate model training for each trait. Human-guided schema development offers a path to extend pxGPT to other crops and imaging conditions, with accuracy requiring validation in each new setting.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The software is available at https://github.com/YaoChengLab/pxgpt and an archival version of the source code is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22931745). Curated schemas used in this study, annotation guides, phenotype records and human annotations are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907554.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag781.summary: We present Phenotype eXplorer Generative Plant Traits (pxGPT), a Python framework that converts multi-view plant images into structured phenotype records.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag781.title: pxGPT: A schema-constrained multimodal LLM framework for plant phenotyping

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag782.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Ancient DNA (aDNA) research has advanced rapidly with the development of high-throughput sequencing, enabling genome-wide analyses of large collections of prehistoric specimens. However, analysing palaeontological and archaeological material with highly degraded DNA constitutes a major bioinformatic challenge. DNA from such samples is characterized by short fragment lengths, low endogenous content, post-mortem damage, and cross-species contamination, which can increase spurious mapping and reference bias, affecting downstream population genetic inferences.

RESULTS: We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens. DNAharvester integrates metagenomic filtering, competitive mapping, adaptive aligner selection (incorporating BWA-aln, BWA-mem, and Bowtie2), and systematic evaluation of reference bias and spurious mapping. By incorporating flexible mapping and filtering strategies, the pipeline can be adapted to varying sample preservation, focusing on maximizing authentic data recovery. DNAharvester features subworkflows for iterative assembly of mitogenomes, identification of genomic repeats and CpG sites, taxonomic classification, microbial/pathogen screening, genetic sex determination, and variant calling. To accommodate varying sequencing depths, the pipeline supports diploid variant calling, genotype likelihood estimation, and pseudo-haploid random allele calling. We validated the pipeline using simulated and empirical datasets, demonstrating its ability to systematically mitigate complex background contamination while preserving authentic genomic signals. By streamlining complex bioinformatic tasks through simple configuration files, DNAharvester establishes a standardized approach for analysing aDNA datasets and makes genomic analyses of ancient remains accessible to the broader research community.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Implemented in Nextflow, DNAharvester provides a highly scalable, containerized framework that enhances reproducibility, portability, and robustness in aDNA analyses. DNAharvester is open source under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and freely available at https://github.com/NBISweden/DNAharvester.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online and Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22725211.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag782.summary: We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag782.title: DNAharvester: A Nextflow Pipeline for Analysing Highly Degraded DNA from Ancient and Historical Specimens

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag783.abstract:
SUMMARY: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) information from one's own dataset is considered optimal for downstream analyses such as statistical fine-mapping. However, the computational complexity (≈N22 computations for N variants) lead most studies to use external reference panels, such as from 1000 Genomes. To capture LD across all variant pairs in biobank-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets with hundreds of millions of variants, new computational strategies are essential. We present a novel approach that uses multi-GPU distributed computing to compute R2 for every variant pair in a dataset. On chromosome 22 (1.8 million variants) of the 30x WGS 1000 Genomes dataset, our method using eight consumer-level 12GB GPUs (NVIDIA RTX 2080TIs) takes <10 minutes, while the same calculation with PLINK using a high-end 64-threaded CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6338) takes > 80 minutes, corresponding to a ≈8x speedup. We further demonstrate true biobank-scale performance in the Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; 57,170 samples), computing chromosome 1 LD (≈1.38 million variants) in 49 minutes versus 22.7 hours for PLINK, a ≈28x speedup. With this method, we successfully computed on the aforementioned 30x WGS 1000 Genomes dataset (≈120 million variants and ≈2500 samples) the entire LD matrix ($>$1e16, or 10 quadrillion elements) in under 6 hours using 512 NVIDIA 40GB A100 GPUs on the Department of Energy Argonne Leadership Computing Facility Polaris Supercomputer. We make this tool, coded in Python using CuPy, publicly available. Using this tool, researchers can leverage the full extent of their genomic data without relying on external LD reference panels and acquire more accurate, population-specific findings, particularly for groups underrepresented in existing databases.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: ARCHER-LD is an open-source tool available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/rachitk/ARCHER-LD. The version of record used in this manuscript is archived via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23399887.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary material is available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag783.summary: We present a novel approach that uses multi-GPU distributed computing to compute R2 for every variant pair in a dataset.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag783.title: ARCHER-LD: Rapid Long-Range Linkage Disequilibrium Calculations at Biobank Scale using GPU Acceleration

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag784.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis is foundational for interpreting RNA sequencing data, but it conflates direct biological effects with correlations propagated through gene co-expression. Across three RNA sequencing datasets (including a genome-scale perturb-seq experiment), we find that only a small fraction of differentially expressed genes have direct effects on the trait of interest, while the majority are undirected or passengers whose associations are mediated through other genes.

RESULTS: To distinguish direct effect genes, we introduce conditional differential gene expression (CDGE) analysis, a framework that tests for conditional rather than marginal association between each gene and the trait of interest. Implemented via the GhostKnockoff procedure with lasso regression, CDGE delivers false discovery rate control, operates on summary statistics from existing DGE pipelines, and accommodates batch effects. The genes identified by CDGE mediate the effects of most other differentially expressed genes and show stronger enrichment for known protein-protein interactions and biological pathways than DGE-identified genes. These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development.

AVAILABILITY: To facilitate public access to knockoff-based CDGE analysis, we have developed the R package "KnockoffCDGE" as an integrated implementation, which is freely available at https://github.com/GuJQ5/KnockoffCDGE (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241517).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag784.summary: These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag784.title: Distilling Direct Effects via Conditional Differential Gene Expression Analysis

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag785.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints.

RESULTS: Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design.

AVAILABILITY: The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag785.summary: Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag785.title: DNA-BFN: Bayesian Flow Networks for Generative Modeling of Regulatory DNA Sequences

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag786.abstract:
MOTIVATION: The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control.

RESULTS: We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualising mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR.

AVAILABILITY: Accessible at https://mardy.net.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag786.summary: We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag786.title: MARDy 2.0: a platform for exploring and analysing antifungal resistance mutations

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag787.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways play a central role in host health, but studying them is limited by the data available. Large clinical microbiome cohorts often lack metabolomic measurements, while multi-omics studies with paired profiles are typically small or incompletely phenotyped. Combining such complementary datasets is challenging: the metabolite is not measured in the clinical cohort, microbiome data are high-dimensional and compositional, and log-ratio analyses depend on an arbitrarily chosen reference taxon.

RESULTS: We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome-metabolome profiles. A high-dimensional structural equation model jointly links the microbiome, the metabolome and the disease outcome. It allows for unmeasured confounding and groups microbes into functional categories. We address compositionality with the additive log-ratio (ALR) transformation, estimate parameters by penalized two-stage least squares, and test metabolite-disease associations with a regularized permutation test. A novel multiple-reference procedure treats each microbe in turn as the ALR reference. It combines the resulting p-values with the Cauchy combination test and classifies microbes by stability selection, which makes inference robust to the choice of reference. In simulations, the method controls the type I error rate, and its power increases with both target and external sample sizes. An application to inflammatory bowel disease, integrating the FRAN and iHMP cohorts, reveals biologically interpretable microbiome-metabolome-disease links.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The method is implemented in the R package MMDP, freely available at https://github.com/lei-fang-stat/MMDP.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag787.summary: We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome-metabolome profiles.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag787.title: Integrating complementary datasets for constructing microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag788.abstract:
SUMMARY: Human genetic evidence provides a strong foundation for selecting drug targets. However, consistent benchmarking of target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes has been hindered by proprietary data and customised pipelines. To address this, we present the Python package ct-validation, which evaluates whether target-indication pairs supported by specific evidence sources are enriched for clinical progression.This package computes relative success (RS) and odds ratios (OR) with confidence intervals across clinical phase transitions. It also supports ontology-based semantic disease matching and offers interfaces in Python, on the command line, and via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By remapping the benchmark from Minikel et al. (2024) to the Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO), we reproduced their per-transition enrichment, with a maximum difference of only 1.4% across any transition.In a systematic 3x3 benchmark that independently varies the genetic evidence and clinical trial sources, we found that a single curated open clinical trial source reproduces the signal of the proprietary comparator (RS = 2.92 vs 2.65; 2.34 vs 2.55 without oncology). However, aggregating open clinical trial registries compresses this signal (RS = 1.52); this loss is primarily driven by the breadth of the indication data rather than the genetic evidence.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: ct-validation is implemented in Python (version 3.11 or higher), distributed via pip, and freely available at https://github.com/gero-science/ct-validation, with support for Python, command-line, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901497. Benchmark data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901451.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag788.summary: However, aggregating open clinical trial registries compresses this signal (RS = 1.52); this loss is primarily driven by the breadth of the indication data rather than the genetic evidence.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag788.title: ct-validation: an open framework for benchmarking target–indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag789.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Predicted protein structure resources now contain hundreds of millions of models, turning structural comparison from a pairwise alignment task into a database-scale retrieval problem. Exhaustive structural aligners are computationally impractical at this scale, whereas fast structural-alphabet searches may discard remote or low-complexity homologs during prefiltering. Database-scale search therefore requires methods that combine rapid retrieval with sensitivity to global structural similarity.

RESULTS: We present SSAlign, a protein structure search method that integrates SaProt sequence-structure embeddings, entropy-reduced dense retrieval, an SS-score predictor and two-stage alignment refinement. In benchmarks on the Swiss-Prot, SCOPe40 and AFDB50 datasets, SSAlign showed competitive alignment quality and returned more TM-align-supported hits than Foldseek in recall-oriented evaluations. On AFDB50, 1,000 queries against 53.7 million structures completed in 3,150 s on CPUs and 2,290 s with GPU prefiltering, corresponding to 103-fold and 142-fold speedups over Foldseek, respectively. On SCOPe40, SSAlign increased the area under the curve (AUC) by 20.2% at family level and 33.3% at superfamily level. In simple-fold antimicrobial peptide case studies, SSAlign retrieved candidates that were not returned by Foldseek under the tested settings, indicating its utility as a fast candidate-generation tool for proteome-scale structural search.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code for SSAlign is publicly available at https://github.com/ISYSLAB-HUST/SSAlign. The software version and test data used in this study are archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23432919. Datasets and prebuilt indices can be downloaded from http://bioinfo.isyslab.info/ssalign/download/section/ssalign/.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag789.summary: We present SSAlign, a protein structure search method that integrates SaProt sequence-structure embeddings, entropy-reduced dense retrieval, an SS-score predictor and two-stage alignment refinement.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag789.title: SSAlign: Fast and Sensitive Protein Structure Search at Scale

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag790.abstract:
SUMMARY: Most human genes produce multiple RNA isoforms, yet it remains unclear which isoforms are translated into stable, functional proteins. Long-read RNA sequencing resolves full-length transcript structures and, when paired with mass spectrometry, can provide empirical evidence of isoform translation. Despite this opportunity, comprehensive workflows integrating isoform discovery, open reading frame prediction, peptide identification, and protein inference remain limited, leaving users to handle these steps piecemeal. Here, we present LRP2, a modular, end-to-end long-read proteogenomics pipeline built in Nextflow. LRP2 scales transcript discovery to hundreds of samples via PacBio's latest Isocall tool, removes technical artifacts with SQANTI QC, generates and classifies predicted proteomes via CPAT and SQANTI Protein, performs multi-group differential expression and usage analysis via edgeR, DRIMSeq, and a long-read adaptation of LeafCutter, and integrates protein-level evidence from DDA and DIA MS data through FragPipe. For cross-dataset comparison of novel isoforms, LRP2 employs deterministic splice-junction, coordinate-based isoform identifiers. Used as an integrated pipeline, LRP2 enables the detection of novel peptides and improves protein isoform inference to confirm protein isoform translation.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: LRP2 is freely available as a modular Nextflow pipeline at https://github.com/sheynkman-lab/LRP2 (v2.0.0, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22795865). LRP2 supports Docker, Apptainer/Singularity, and Conda environments with GENCODE references.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag790.summary: Here, we present LRP2, a modular, end-to-end long-read proteogenomics pipeline built in Nextflow.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag790.title: LRP2: A proteogenomics pipeline for long-read informed protein isoform analysis and discovery

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag791.abstract:
SUMMARY: DNA methylation microarrays enable cost-effective, high-throughput profiling of human and mouse samples and are widely used to study epigenetic alterations in cancer. Patient-Derived Xenograft (PDX) models complement this approach by preserving primary tumor characteristics while enabling in vivo studies of drug response and therapy resistance. However, it remains difficult to quantify mouse DNA contamination in PDX DNA methylation data generated using microarrays. We present XenoMix, a light-weight computational tool for quantifying mouse DNA contamination directly from DNA methylation data in PDX models. XenoMix leverages the high sequence homology between human and mouse genomes to detect and quantify unexpected signal contributions originating from mouse DNA. Using ground truth mixtures, XenoMix achieved Pearson's correlation coefficients higher than 0.99. When applied to PDX data, we identified varying levels of mouse contamination originating from biological and technological variability. XenoMix establishes a critical quality control step in DNA methylation analysis of PDX models, and we show that the estimated contamination can be incorporated as a confounding variable in downstream analyses.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: XenoMix is available as a standalone R package from https://git.dkfz.de/b370/scepigen/XenoMix and as a module in the RnBeads software package.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag791.summary: We present XenoMix, a light-weight computational tool for quantifying mouse DNA contamination directly from DNA methylation data in PDX models.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag791.title: XenoMix: Estimating mouse content from DNA methylation data of Patient-Derived Xenograft models

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag792.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Accurate somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) calling from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing remains challenging because sequencing errors, variable tumor purity, tumor-in-normal contamination, and low variant allele fractions (VAFs) can obscure tumor-specific signals. Although recent deep-learning methods have improved long-read somatic variant calling, robust low-VAF detection and efficient genome-scale analysis remain important methodological challenges.

RESULTS: We present SomatiX, a deep-learning method for somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing data, built on an allele-aware pileup representation. In comprehensive cancer benchmark analyses across diverse cell-line datasets, sequencing contexts, VAF bins, and minimum variant-supporting read thresholds, SomatiX outperformed DeepSomatic and ClairS in F1 score across most Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) benchmark conditions and achieved competitive performance on Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) data. Across the held-out chromosome 1 cancer cell-line benchmarks, at the threshold of ≥ 3 variant-supporting reads and VAF ≥0.05, SomatiX achieved mean F1 scores of 0.986 for ONT data and 0.988 for PacBio data. SomatiX showed particularly strong performance for low-VAF SNVs in ONT data while using a compact model and achieving the fastest runtime among the evaluated tools.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: SomatiX is available at https://github.com/colinliuzelin/SomatiX and archived at Zenodo under DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22062438. The repository includes source code, trained models, and benchmarking scripts.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag792.summary: We present SomatiX, a deep-learning method for somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing data, built on an allele-aware pileup representation.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag792.title: SomatiX: accurate and efficient somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag793.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Accurate prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity is fundamental to therapeutic design and the rapid response to evolving pathogens. However, current computational approaches predominantly formulate this as a point-wise regression task. This paradigm struggles to discriminate subtle affinity differences among highly homologous variants and lacks the global context necessary to effectively prioritize top-tier candidates. Furthermore, the field is severely constrained by label sparsity. Although sequence data is abundant, experimentally verified affinities are scarce, leaving a massive pool of unverified antibody-antigen structural interactions unexploited by standard supervised paradigms.

RESULTS: We propose AbLWR (Antibody-antigen binding affinity Listwise Ranking), a novel framework that reformulates the conventional affinity regression task as a listwise ranking problem to directly optimize candidate prioritization. To mitigate label sparsity, AbLWR incorporates a Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning mechanism, leveraging a dual-level contrastive objective and meta-optimized label refinement to distill robust structural representations from vast unlabeled data. To accommodate antigenic variation, we employ a homologous antigen sampling strategy coupled with a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) module, which explicitly models inter-sample dependencies within training lists to capture subtle affinity nuances. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AbLWR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art sequence-, structure-, and complex-based baselines. It improves the Full Rank Accuracy (FRA) by approximately 8% compared to the strongest baseline in randomized cross-validation, and exhibits strong robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios involving distinct antigen and antibody clusters. Case studies on Influenza Viruses and Human Interleukin-33 further validate its practical utility. Specifically, AbLWR successfully tracks affinity drops caused by antigenic drift and immediately captures optimal binders in simulated wet-lab screening.

AVAILABILITY: Source code and datasets are freely available at https://github.com/Josie-xufan/AbLWR.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag793.summary: We propose AbLWR (Antibody-antigen binding affinity Listwise Ranking), a novel framework that reformulates the conventional affinity regression task as a listwise ranking problem to directly optimize candidate prioritization.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag793.title: AbLWR: A Context-Aware Listwise Ranking Framework for Antibody-Antigen Binding Affinity Prediction via Positive-Unlabeled Learning

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag794.abstract:
MOTIVATION: The exponential growth of biomedical literature has made automatic indexing essential for advancing biomedical research. While automatic indexing has made strides in English biomedical literature, there has been limited research on non-English biomedical texts due to insufficient high-quality training data.

RESULTS: We propose BERTDeCS, a novel deep learning framework for automatically indexing Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning. BERTDeCS utilizes a multilingual BERT (M-BERT) to generate multi-language representations and adapts M-BERT for Spanish biomedical literature domain through contrastive learning. Additionally, BERTDeCS enhances its semantic indexing capabilities on Spanish biomedical literature by leveraging enriched English annotated literature in MEDLINE through transfer learning. Experimental results on Spanish datasets demonstrate that BERTDeCS outperforms state-of-the-art indexing methods, achieving top performance in the MESINESP and MESINESP2 Tasks on medical semantic indexing in Spanish within the BioASQ challenge. Additional experiments on Portuguese provide preliminary evidence that BERTDeCS can transfer to a closely related language sharing substantial lexical and biomedical terminology with Spanish.

AVAILABILITY: The source code is available at https://github.com/yourh/BERTDeCS and at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23212468.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag794.summary: We propose BERTDeCS, a novel deep learning framework for automatically indexing Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag794.title: Large-scale semantic indexing of Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag795.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Biomedical question answering often requires evidence beyond topically retrieved literature, including gene alias resolution, database identifier normalization, and atlas-derived biological measurements. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically follow a fixed workflow and lack an explicit mechanism for deciding when retrieved text is sufficient, when biomedical entity mapping is needed, or when executable evidence assembly over structured measurements should be invoked. This motivates a substrate-aware large language model (LLM) harness that selectively assembles sufficient evidence by combining literature retrieval, biomedical entity mapping, and access to atlas-derived measurements.

RESULTS: We introduce BioHarness, an LLM harness for staged biomedical evidence assembly across literature retrieval, biomedical entity-mapping resources, and atlas-derived structured measurements. Across 22,123 biomedical QA items spanning seven answer formats, BioHarness improves the pooled score from 62.2 to 67.2 over the strongest baseline. Ablations, case studies, and backbone-scaling analyses show that these gains arise from repairing evidence-substrate mismatches through reranking, entity grounding, and structured measurement access, rather than from indiscriminately invoking more reasoning steps, retrieving additional literature, or relying on a particular answer-model scale. Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus lookup.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag795.summary: Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus…
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag795.title: BioHarness: Substrate-Aware Evidence Assembly for Biomedical Question Answering across Literature, Knowledge Bases, and Biological Atlases

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag796.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Existing pangenome file formats are designed for batch processing. Graphs must be loaded into memory, and alignment files must be read sequentially. Indexed file formats that can be used directly from disk would be more appropriate for interactive applications.

RESULTS: We propose GBZ-base and GAF-base - SQLite-backed file formats comparable to GBZ and GAF. GBZ-base supports efficient extraction of local subgraphs, and GAF-base lets us extract all alignments to the subgraph. Additionally, GAF-base is smaller than any other file format for sequence-to-graph alignments.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: From https://github.com/jltsiren/gbz-base and https://crates.io/crates/gbz-base under the MIT license.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag796.summary: We propose GBZ-base and GAF-base - SQLite-backed file formats comparable to GBZ and GAF.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag796.title: GBZ-base and GAF-base: Indexed pangenome file formats

10.1093/bioinformatics/btag797.abstract:
MOTIVATION: CircRNA-miRNA interactions (CMIs) play regulatory roles in human diseases and provide clues for therapeutic target discovery. However, most existing prediction methods rely on circRNA-miRNA pairs and overlook disease-level regulatory contexts, which limits their ability to characterize cross-pathway dependencies in zero-shot inference.

RESULTS: We propose MV-S2M, a multi-view state-space modeling framework that integrates molecular attributes to enhance relational reasoning, enabling zero-shot CMI prediction. Specifically, MV-S2M performs structure-aware diffusion to enrich molecular priors and constructs disease-mediated semantic subgraphs. It then incorporates state-space modeling to capture long-range dependencies and view-specific regulatory patterns. The learned multi-view representations are fused through a linear projection and fed into an MLP for CMI prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that MV-S2M achieves state-of-the-art performance under both zero-shot and conventional settings. Cold-start evaluations reveal distinct generalization behavior across different unseen-entity settings. Case studies illustrate the contribution of meta-path-guided semantic subgraphs to CMI prediction.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/591286260/MV and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22858403.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag797.summary: We propose MV-S2M, a multi-view state-space modeling framework that integrates molecular attributes to enhance relational reasoning, enabling zero-shot CMI prediction.
10.1093/bioinformatics/btag797.title: Multi-View State-Space Modeling for Zero-Shot circRNA-miRNA Interaction Prediction

10.1126/science.adt1992.abstract: The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. In this work, we report on a sizable thermal Hall conductivity in nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS3), a van der Waals stack of honeycomb layers with a zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The longitudinal (κaa) and the transverse (κab) thermal conductivities peak at the same temperature, and the thermal Hall angle, at this peak, respects a previously identified bound. The amplitude of κab is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the b axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.
10.1126/science.adt1992.summary: The amplitude of κab is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the b axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.
10.1126/science.adt1992.title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet

10.1126/science.adt9825.abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd5AlI2, a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd5AlI2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.
10.1126/science.adt9825.summary: Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.
10.1126/science.adt9825.title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal

10.1126/science.ady8560.abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.
10.1126/science.ady8560.summary: We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate.
10.1126/science.ady8560.title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity

10.1126/science.aea2181.abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. Activation of BAX-BAK without apoptosome activation triggers sustained efflux of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and caspase-independent cell death. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation-induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.
10.1126/science.aea2181.summary: These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.
10.1126/science.aea2181.title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death

10.1126/science.aea7156.abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.
10.1126/science.aea7156.summary: These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.
10.1126/science.aea7156.title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer

10.1126/science.aed3379.abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.
10.1126/science.aed3379.summary: Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation.
10.1126/science.aed3379.title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet

10.1126/science.aed5772.abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) threatens terrestrial biodiversity, yet its spatiotemporal and species-specific impacts remain unclear. Integrating relative SLR projections across five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with area of habitat (AOH) maps for 34,120 terrestrial vertebrate species, we project that species exposed to SLR will increase from up to 13,680 in 2050 to 15,324 by 2100, including 57 to 63% of birds, 47 to 52% of mammals, 28 to 36% of reptiles, and 20 to 24% of amphibians. In Southeast Asia, inland inundation areas support high richness. Under SSP5-8.5, species facing >10% habitat inundation surge from 18 in 2050 to 109 by 2100, with reptiles and already threatened species overrepresented. Safeguarding SLR refugia-the noninundated habitats for exposed species-is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.
10.1126/science.aed5772.summary: Safeguarding SLR refugia-the noninundated habitats for exposed species-is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.
10.1126/science.aed5772.title: Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise

10.1126/science.aed6459.abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows (Corvus corone) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.
10.1126/science.aed6459.summary: We show that carrion crows (Corvus corone) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without…
10.1126/science.aed6459.title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain

10.1126/science.aed8319.abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.
10.1126/science.aed8319.summary: Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.
10.1126/science.aed8319.title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels

10.1126/science.aee6967.abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°-twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.
10.1126/science.aee6967.summary: This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.
10.1126/science.aee6967.title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals

10.1126/science.aef0940.abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter's states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra-unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.
10.1126/science.aef0940.summary: We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.
10.1126/science.aef0940.title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting

10.1126/science.aef9745.abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization. The certified PCE with phenethylammonium iodide as the passivation molecule was 20.2% on PSMs with device areas of 750 cm2. With 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide as the passivator, the PCE of 22.0% for a device area of 14.55 cm2 decreased by 8% after 1044 hours under maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices pass all sequences of an international commercialization assessment standard for flexible portable PSMs.
10.1126/science.aef9745.summary: We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization.
10.1126/science.aef9745.title: Decoupled self-assembled monolayer and perovskite deposition for efficient flexible solar modules

10.1126/science.aeg1821.abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.
10.1126/science.aeg1821.summary: Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.
10.1126/science.aeg1821.title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria

10.1126/science.aeg6779.abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.
10.1126/science.aeg6779.summary: We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points.
10.1126/science.aeg6779.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development

10.1126/science.aeh7930.abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.
10.1126/science.aeh7930.summary: We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests.
10.1126/science.aeh7930.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models

10.1126/science.aek5696.abstract: The genomic regions regulating gene expression are often themselves transcribed into a variety of noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs). However, the regulatory roles of this noncoding transcription remain largely unknown. By using live imaging, we reveal that the sequential transcription of ncRNAs emanating from distinct regulatory elements underlies gene activation in Drosophila embryos. Single-allele covisualization uncovers that optimal gene activation is achieved by only moderate levels of enhancer activity. Disrupting enhancer-associated ncRNAs causes precocious gene activation, providing evidence that ncRNAs control the timing of gene expression in development. We further show that enhancer transcription can regulate long-range interactions within complex regulatory landscapes. We propose that ncRNAs locally modulate regulatory element activity in cis to shape genome organization and orchestrate the temporal control of gene expression in development.
10.1126/science.aek5696.summary: We propose that ncRNAs locally modulate regulatory element activity in cis to shape genome organization and orchestrate the temporal control of gene expression in development.
10.1126/science.aek5696.title: Noncoding transcription controls the developmental dynamics of long-range gene regulation
